Countries that grow coffee.Brazil: Brazil has led world coffee output for over 150 years and supplies roughly a third of all beans grown on Earth.
Countries that grow coffee.Colombia: Colombian coffee is marketed by the fictional farmer Juan Valdez, a mascot created in 1958 that became a national symbol.
Countries that grow coffee.Ethiopia: Coffee is said to have been discovered here, when a goatherd named Kaldi noticed his goats dancing after eating red berries.
Countries that grow coffee.Vietnam: Vietnam is the world's biggest producer of robusta and second overall, and it serves it strong with sweetened condensed milk.
Countries that grow coffee.Kenya: Kenya's high-altitude farms produce bright, berry-like beans, and its auction system rewards the best lots with top prices.
Countries that grow coffee.Guatemala: Volcanic soil and mountain shade give Guatemalan coffee a smoky, chocolatey depth; Antigua is its most famous growing region.
Countries that grow coffee.Costa Rica: Costa Rica banned robusta by law in 1989, so every bean grown there is the higher-quality arabica variety.
Countries that grow coffee.Honduras: Honduras is one of Central America's biggest coffee exporters, with most of it grown by small family farms in the mountains.
Countries that grow coffee.Indonesia: Indonesia's Sumatra beans are often wet-hulled, giving an earthy flavor, and Java was so important that it became slang for coffee.
Countries that grow coffee.Jamaica: Jamaica's Blue Mountain coffee is among the world's priciest and is shipped in special wooden barrels instead of sacks.
Countries that grow coffee.Yemen: Yemen's port of Mocha gave its name to the coffee-and-chocolate drink, and Yemenis were trading coffee centuries ago.
Countries that grow coffee.Peru: Peru is a leading source of organic and fair-trade coffee, grown by small farms on Andean slopes.
Countries that grow coffee.Rwanda: Rwanda's coffee industry rebuilt after the 1994 genocide, and its washed beans now fetch specialty prices worldwide.
Countries that grow coffee.Italy: Italy invented espresso culture and the espresso machine, yet its climate is wrong for growing beans; it only roasts and drinks them.
Countries that grow coffee.France: France gave the world the French press and café culture, but its climate is too cold for coffee at home; it grows it only in overseas territories.
Countries that grow coffee.Austria: Viennese coffeehouses are on UNESCO's intangible heritage list, but all of Austria's beans have to be imported.
Countries that grow coffee.Turkey: Turkey is famous for its thick, cezve-brewed coffee, but its climate can't grow the plant, so it imports every bean.
Countries that grow coffee.Sweden: Swedes drink some of the most coffee per person on Earth and have the fika break, but the plant can't survive Swedish winters.
Countries that grow coffee.Finland: Finns drink more coffee per person than almost anyone, around 10 kilos of beans a year, yet none grows in the Arctic cold.
Countries that grow coffee.Germany: Germany is a major coffee importer and roaster, but its climate makes growing the tropical plant impossible outdoors.
Countries that grow coffee.Netherlands: Dutch traders helped spread coffee plants to colonies in Java and the Americas, but the home country is too cold to grow any.
Countries that grow coffee.Norway: Norwegians drink among the most coffee per capita in the world, yet the plant needs frost-free tropics that Norway lacks.
Countries that grow coffee.Canada: Canada runs on coffee chains like Tim Hortons, but coffee needs a frost-free climate that is found only in tropical belts.
Countries that grow coffee.Denmark: Danes are heavy coffee drinkers, but Denmark is a pure importer, with no climate for coffee plants outdoors.

Landforms.Mesa: Spanish for table, a mesa is a flat-topped hill with steep sides, left standing as softer rock around it erodes away.
Landforms.Butte: A butte is a mesa's smaller cousin, narrow and steep-sided; Monument Valley's famous buttes tower roughly 300 meters above the desert floor.
Landforms.Plateau: The Tibetan Plateau averages over 4,500 meters in height and is often called the roof of the world.
Landforms.Canyon: The Grand Canyon is about 446 kilometers long, and the Colorado River cut it over millions of years.
Landforms.Valley: Glaciers carve U-shaped valleys while rivers carve V-shaped ones, so the cross-section reveals what shaped it.
Landforms.Peninsula: Land surrounded by water on three sides; the Arabian Peninsula is the largest in the world, about three million square kilometers.
Landforms.Isthmus: A narrow land bridge joining two larger lands. Panama's isthmus linked North and South America and split the Atlantic from the Pacific.
Landforms.Delta: River deltas get their name from the Greek letter, because the Nile's mouth looked like a triangle. Many are among the most fertile land.
Landforms.Fjord: A glacier-carved valley flooded by the sea. Some, like Norway's Sognefjord, are over 1,000 meters deep.
Landforms.Dune: Sand dunes can sing: when sand avalanches down certain slopes, grains vibrate to produce a deep humming sound.
Landforms.Volcano: Hawaii's Mauna Loa is the largest active volcano on Earth, and most of its mass sits below the ocean surface.
Landforms.Cliff: The Cliffs of Moher in Ireland rise about 120 meters and stretch for roughly 14 kilometers along the Atlantic.
Landforms.Plain: Plains cover about a third of Earth's land and feed much of humanity; the Great Plains of North America once held vast bison herds.
Landforms.Tsunami: A wave, not a landform. Tsunamis can cross an entire ocean at jet speed, and in deep water they are barely noticeable.
Landforms.Monsoon: A seasonal wind shift that brings months of heavy rain, not a landform. Over a billion people rely on its rains for farming.
Landforms.Tide: The sea's rise and fall is a process, not a landform. The Bay of Fundy sees the world's biggest tidal range, up to about 16 meters.
Landforms.Equator: An imaginary line, not a landform. It crosses only a few countries and is about 40,000 kilometers long.
Landforms.Aurora: A glow in the sky, not a landform. It happens when particles from the sun excite gases in the upper atmosphere.
Landforms.Hurricane: A storm, not a landform. Hurricanes are called typhoons in the western Pacific and cyclones in the Indian Ocean.
Landforms.Latitude: An imaginary line measuring distance north or south of the equator, not a landform. Each degree spans about 111 kilometers.
Landforms.Avalanche: A sliding mass of snow is an event, not a landform. Big ones can reach speeds above 100 kilometers per hour.
Landforms.Earthquake: A shaking of the ground, an event rather than a landform, though quakes can create new cliffs and valleys.
Landforms.Meridian: A north-south imaginary line, not a landform. The prime meridian passes through Greenwich, England, by an 1884 international agreement.
Landforms.Tornado: A rotating air column, not a landform. The US sees about 1,000 a year, more than any other country.

Dinosaurs.Tyrannosaurus: Its bite was among the strongest of any land animal ever, and its bone-crushing teeth were about the size of bananas.
Dinosaurs.Triceratops: Its skull could reach about 2 meters, a third of its body length, and it lived in the very last days of the dinosaurs.
Dinosaurs.Stegosaurus: Its brain was famously small, roughly walnut sized, and the purpose of its back plates is still debated.
Dinosaurs.Velociraptor: The real animal was only turkey-sized and feathered, much smaller than the movie version.
Dinosaurs.Brachiosaurus: Its front legs were longer than its back legs, giving a giraffe-like posture, and it could reach treetops about 12 meters high.
Dinosaurs.Diplodocus: Its whip-like tail may have cracked above the speed of sound, and it stretched about 25 meters.
Dinosaurs.Ankylosaurus: Armored with bony plates and a club tail, it could break the bones of an attacker with one swing.
Dinosaurs.Spinosaurus: The biggest known meat-eating dinosaur was a semi-aquatic hunter with a sail on its back and a crocodile-like snout.
Dinosaurs.Iguanodon: One of the first dinosaurs ever named, in 1825; its thumb spike was at first mistakenly placed on its nose.
Dinosaurs.Allosaurus: A top predator of the Jurassic, it may have hunted in groups and was about 8 meters long.
Dinosaurs.Parasaurolophus: The hollow crest on its head could work like a trombone, producing low-pitched calls to communicate.
Dinosaurs.Pachycephalosaurus: Its name means thick-headed lizard, and its skull dome was up to 25 centimeters thick, perhaps for head-butting.
Dinosaurs.Pterodactyl: A trap: pterosaurs flew, and they were reptiles related to dinosaurs, not dinosaurs themselves.
Dinosaurs.Plesiosaur: A marine reptile with a long neck and flippers, not a dinosaur; the Loch Ness monster is often imagined as one.
Dinosaurs.Mosasaurus: A giant marine lizard that ruled the seas near the end of the dinosaur age, related to modern monitor lizards, not dinosaurs.
Dinosaurs.Ichthyosaur: A dolphin-shaped sea reptile that gave birth to live young, and not a dinosaur.
Dinosaurs.Dimetrodon: This sail-backed predator lived before the dinosaurs and is actually closer kin to mammals than to reptiles.
Dinosaurs.Woolly mammoth: A mammal from the Ice Age, tens of millions of years after the dinosaurs died out; pygmy mammoths survived on an island until about 4,000 years ago.
Dinosaurs.Smilodon: The saber-toothed cat was an Ice Age mammal, and lived millions of years after the dinosaurs died out.
Dinosaurs.Megalodon: A giant shark, not a dinosaur: it lived millions of years after the dinosaurs vanished, and it could reach about 15 meters long.
Dinosaurs.Komodo dragon: The largest living lizard is a reptile, not a dinosaur, and its bite delivers venom.
Dinosaurs.Dodo: A flightless bird from Mauritius that went extinct in the 1600s; birds are the dinosaurs' living descendants, but the dodo itself isn't a dinosaur.
Dinosaurs.Mastodon: A trap: this elephant relative lived in the Ice Age, tens of millions of years after the dinosaurs.
Dinosaurs.Quetzalcoatlus: One of the largest flying animals ever, with a wingspan of about 10 meters, but a pterosaur, not a dinosaur.

Animals with quills or spines.Porcupine: A porcupine carries about 30,000 quills, and they detach easily on contact. Contrary to myth, it cannot shoot them.
Animals with quills or spines.Hedgehog: A hedgehog's spines are hollow, modified hairs, and it rolls into a tight ball when scared. It may also self-anoint, smearing frothy saliva on them.
Animals with quills or spines.Echidna: Echidnas are egg-laying mammals, with spines that are really stiff hairs. A single egg is carried in a belly pouch.
Animals with quills or spines.Sea urchin: Sea urchins have spines on a shell called a test, and their mouth is a five-toothed jaw known as Aristotle's lantern.
Animals with quills or spines.Pufferfish: When threatened, a pufferfish gulps water to swell into a ball and erect its spines. Its organs hold a toxin far deadlier than cyanide.
Animals with quills or spines.Lionfish: Lionfish wear venomous dorsal spines like a fan. Native to the Indo-Pacific, they became a damaging invasive species in the Atlantic.
Animals with quills or spines.Tenrec: Tenrecs of Madagascar look like hedgehogs, but they are only distant relatives. Some species even rub their quills together to make sound.
Animals with quills or spines.Crown-of-thorns: This starfish is covered in venomous spines and devours coral reefs. A single one can eat several square metres of coral each year.
Animals with quills or spines.Thorny devil: The thorny devil is an Australian lizard covered in spikes. Tiny grooves in its skin channel dew and rain straight to its mouth.
Animals with quills or spines.Armadillo: Armadillos trade spines for armour: bony plates in the skin. Only the three-banded kinds can roll into a full ball, and some always give birth to identical quadruplets.
Animals with quills or spines.Pangolin: Pangolins are covered in keratin scales, not spines, the same material as your fingernails. They are among the most trafficked mammals on Earth.
Animals with quills or spines.Turtle: A turtle's shell is bone fused to its ribs and spine, so it can't leave it. There are no quills or spines to be found.
Animals with quills or spines.Rhino: A rhino's horn is made of keratin, the stuff of hair and nails, not bone. It's a solid mass, so it's no spine or quill.
Animals with quills or spines.Shark: Sharks wear tiny tooth-like denticles instead of spines, giving skin that feels like sandpaper. Some dogfish do have spines at their dorsal fins, though.
Animals with quills or spines.Skunk: Skunks defend themselves with spray, not spines. They can aim it accurately up to about three metres, and they usually warn first.
Animals with quills or spines.Raccoon: Raccoons have no spines at all. Their sensitive front paws have thousands of nerve endings, which helps explain the famous washing behaviour.
Animals with quills or spines.Badger: Badgers rely on strong claws and powerful jaws, not spines. They dig elaborate burrows called setts that can last for generations.
Animals with quills or spines.Anteater: Anteaters are often confused with spiny animals, but their coat is coarse hair. A giant anteater's tongue can flick in and out about 150 times a minute.
Animals with quills or spines.Koala: Koalas are soft and furry with no spines. Their fingerprints are so like humans' that they have confused crime-scene investigators.
Animals with quills or spines.Otter: Otters have the densest fur of any animal, up to a million hairs per square inch in sea otters. It's thick fur, not spines, that keeps them warm.
Animals with quills or spines.Crocodile: Crocodiles are armoured with bony osteoderms under thick skin rather than quills. They can go a year or more between meals.
Animals with quills or spines.Beaver: Beavers have a paddle-like tail and constantly growing orange teeth. They are covered in dense fur, with no spines.
Animals with quills or spines.Mole: Moles are velvety diggers with no spines. Their fur lies flat in either direction so they can reverse in tunnels.
Animals with quills or spines.Sloth: Sloths have coarse fur, not spines, and algae grows in it, giving a greenish tint. They descend to the ground about once a week to defecate.

Spices that are seeds.Coriander seed: The same plant as cilantro, but the seeds taste warm and citrusy, not soapy.
Spices that are seeds.Fennel seed: In India the seeds are chewed after meals as a breath freshener.
Spices that are seeds.Mustard seed: Yellow, brown and black varieties release their heat only when crushed and mixed with liquid.
Spices that are seeds.Nutmeg: It's the seed of a tropical tree, and the Banda Islands monopoly led to wars; the Dutch swapped Manhattan for one island in 1667.
Spices that are seeds.Caraway: It flavors rye bread and the liqueur kümmel, and the seeds look like tiny crescents.
Spices that are seeds.Fenugreek: The seeds smell like maple syrup, thanks to the compound sotolon.
Spices that are seeds.Anise seed: The licorice-like flavor of the seeds goes into ouzo, sambuca and absinthe.
Spices that are seeds.Celery seed: They come from wild celery, a different plant, not the stalk celery.
Spices that are seeds.Nigella: Also called kalonji, these black seeds sprinkle over naan and are not a cumin.
Spices that are seeds.Poppy seed: They come from the opium poppy, and eating enough can trigger a positive drug test.
Spices that are seeds.Cinnamon: This is bark, not seed, from the inner layer of a tree, rolled into quills.
Spices that are seeds.Clove: It is a dried flower bud, not a seed, and its name comes from the Latin for nail.
Spices that are seeds.Saffron: The thread-like stigmas of the crocus, hand-picked, which is why it is the costliest spice.
Spices that are seeds.Ginger: A rhizome, or underground stem, and not a seed, and it's used fresh and dried.
Spices that are seeds.Turmeric: A rhizome, which is why it's not a seed, and it gives curry its yellow color and a compound called curcumin.
Spices that are seeds.Paprika: Ground dried peppers, so technically the fruit's flesh rather than the seeds.
Spices that are seeds.Allspice: It's the dried unripe berry of a Caribbean tree, and tastes like cinnamon, nutmeg and clove together.
Spices that are seeds.Star anise: The dried star-shaped fruit pod, which is not a seed, and gets its licorice taste from anethole.
Spices that are seeds.Mace: Mace is the red lacy covering around the nutmeg seed, so it's from the same fruit, but not the seed.
Spices that are seeds.Bay leaf: A leaf, not a seed, from a laurel tree, and removed before serving.
Spices that are seeds.Sumac: Dried, ground fruits of a bush, tangy and used in Middle Eastern dishes, so berries, not seeds.
Spices that are seeds.Garlic powder: It's made from the bulb of garlic, not the seeds, and it is dried and ground.
Spices that are seeds.Lemongrass: The stalks of a tropical grass, which is why it's fresh and citrusy, and no seed.

Islands in the Atlantic Ocean.Bermuda: Bermuda's pink beaches get their color from tiny red shells, and the island sits near the center of the Bermuda Triangle legend.
Islands in the Atlantic Ocean.Azores: The Azores are nine volcanic Portuguese islands, where locals cook a stew, cozido, underground using volcanic heat.
Islands in the Atlantic Ocean.Canary Islands: Teide on Tenerife is the highest peak in Spain at about 3,700 meters, and the islands are named for dogs, not canaries.

Islands in the Atlantic Ocean.Cape Verde: Cape Verde is an island nation off West Africa, and its music, morna, was made famous by Cesária Évora, who sang barefoot.
Islands in the Atlantic Ocean.Madeira: Madeira is known for its fortified wine, which was once shipped on long voyages and improved by the heat.
Islands in the Atlantic Ocean.Falkland Islands: Argentina and Britain fought a war over the Falklands in 1982; there are more sheep on the islands than people.
Islands in the Atlantic Ocean.St Helena: Napoleon was exiled to St Helena in 1815 and died there in 1821; it's among the most remote inhabited islands on Earth.
Islands in the Atlantic Ocean.Faroe Islands: The Faroes belong to Denmark and have far more sheep than people; their name likely means sheep islands.
Islands in the Atlantic Ocean.Ascension Island: Ascension is a remote volcanic island whose green mountain was planted with trees by 19th-century sailors, and it hosts nesting green turtles.
Islands in the Atlantic Ocean.Bahamas: The Bahamas have about 700 islands and cays, and the islands have a famous swimming pig beach.
Islands in the Atlantic Ocean.Newfoundland: Newfoundland is where Vikings built a settlement around 1000 AD, at L'Anse aux Meadows, the first known European site in North America.
Islands in the Atlantic Ocean.Hawaii: Hawaii is in the Pacific, the most remote island chain on Earth.
Islands in the Atlantic Ocean.Fiji: Fiji is in the South Pacific, far away from the Atlantic.
Islands in the Atlantic Ocean.Maldives: The Maldives are in the Indian Ocean, where coral atolls rise barely above the waves.
Islands in the Atlantic Ocean.Seychelles: The Seychelles are in the Indian Ocean, not the Atlantic, and are a nature-lover's haven.
Islands in the Atlantic Ocean.Galápagos: The Galápagos lie in the Pacific, off Ecuador, and their wildlife inspired Darwin.
Islands in the Atlantic Ocean.Tahiti: Tahiti is in the Pacific, and Captain Cook visited it in 1769 to watch Venus cross the Sun.
Islands in the Atlantic Ocean.Mauritius: Mauritius is in the Indian Ocean, and the dodo's island.
Islands in the Atlantic Ocean.Ceylon: Ceylon was the old name of Sri Lanka, in the Indian Ocean, and the name lives on in Ceylon tea.
Islands in the Atlantic Ocean.Guam: Guam is in the western Pacific, and it's a US territory, thousands of kilometers from the Atlantic.
Islands in the Atlantic Ocean.Samoa: Samoa is in the Pacific, and it is where the writer Robert Louis Stevenson spent his last years.
Islands in the Atlantic Ocean.Zanzibar: Zanzibar is in the Indian Ocean, off the coast of Tanzania, and not an Atlantic island.
Islands in the Atlantic Ocean.Bali: Bali is in Indonesia, between the Indian and Pacific Oceans, and it is mostly Hindu in a mostly Muslim country.

Cities in Australia.Sydney: Sydney's Opera House has over a million roof tiles, and was designed by Danish architect Jørn Utzon, who left before it was finished.
Cities in Australia.Melbourne: Melbourne regularly tops livability lists, and it's famous for its coffee, laneways and love of Australian rules football.
Cities in Australia.Brisbane: Brisbane sits on a winding river and has the Lone Pine Koala Sanctuary, the world's first, from 1927.
Cities in Australia.Perth: Perth is among the world's most isolated big cities, with Adelaide over 2,000 km away.
Cities in Australia.Adelaide: Adelaide was planned as a grid ringed by parkland, and is surrounded by wine regions like the Barossa Valley.
Cities in Australia.Hobart: Hobart is Tasmania's capital, Australia's second-oldest city, and the finish of the Sydney to Hobart yacht race.
Cities in Australia.Darwin: Darwin is named for Charles Darwin, and was bombed by Japan in 1942 in the largest attack on Australian soil.
Cities in Australia.Canberra: Canberra, not Sydney or Melbourne, is Australia's capital, a planned city chosen as a compromise between the two rivals.
Cities in Australia.Cairns: Cairns is the gateway to the Great Barrier Reef, the largest coral reef system on Earth, visible from space.
Cities in Australia.Alice Springs: Alice Springs sits at the center of the continent, and it is the nearest town to Uluru, about 450 km away.
Cities in Australia.Gold Coast: The Gold Coast is a strip of surf beaches and high-rises, and has one of the tallest residential buildings, Q1.
Cities in Australia.Auckland: Auckland is in New Zealand and sprawls over about 50 dormant volcanoes.
Cities in Australia.Wellington: Wellington is New Zealand's capital, and is one of the windiest cities in the world.
Cities in Australia.Christchurch: Christchurch is in New Zealand, and rebuilt after the damaging earthquakes of 2010 and 2011.
Cities in Australia.Queenstown: Queenstown, New Zealand, is the adventure capital of the world, and where commercial bungee jumping started in 1988.
Cities in Australia.Dunedin: Dunedin, New Zealand, was settled by Scots, and its name is the old Gaelic name for Edinburgh.
Cities in Australia.Rotorua: Rotorua is in New Zealand, a place of geysers and bubbling mud, rich in Maori culture.
Cities in Australia.Suva: Suva is the capital of Fiji, in the South Pacific, not Australia.
Cities in Australia.Port Moresby: Port Moresby is the capital of Papua New Guinea, which is separated from Australia by the Torres Strait.
Cities in Australia.Nouméa: Nouméa is the capital of New Caledonia, a French territory in the Pacific.
Cities in Australia.Johannesburg: Johannesburg is in South Africa, and grew up from a gold rush in 1886.
Cities in Australia.Vancouver: Vancouver is in Canada, and it often ranks among the world's most livable cities, like Melbourne.
Cities in Australia.Whangarei: Whangarei is New Zealand's northernmost city, in Northland, and sits on a sheltered harbor.
Cities in Australia.Tauranga: Tauranga is in New Zealand, and has one of the country's busiest ports.

Places in Egypt.Pyramids of Giza: The Great Pyramid, built around 2560 BC, was the world's tallest structure for nearly 4,000 years and is the last ancient wonder still standing.
Places in Egypt.Sphinx: Carved from a single limestone outcrop, this lion-bodied guardian probably bears the face of the pharaoh Khafre.
Places in Egypt.Valley of the Kings: Near Luxor, about 60 royal tombs were hidden here, including Tutankhamun's, found nearly intact in 1922.
Places in Egypt.Karnak: This temple complex at Luxor was built over some 2,000 years, and its Great Hypostyle Hall has 134 giant columns.
Places in Egypt.Luxor: Ancient Thebes is often called the world's greatest open-air museum, with temples on one bank and tombs on the other.
Places in Egypt.Abu Simbel: Ramesses II's temples were cut into blocks and moved uphill in the 1960s to escape the rising Aswan High Dam lake.
Places in Egypt.Suez Canal: Opened in 1869, it links the Mediterranean to the Red Sea with no locks, and a 2021 grounding blocked it for six days.
Places in Egypt.Alexandria: Alexander the Great founded it in 331 BC. Its Pharos lighthouse was one of the ancient world's seven wonders.
Places in Egypt.Cairo: Its Arabic name means the victorious. It is the largest city in Africa's Arab world and sits on the Nile.
Places in Egypt.Sinai: This triangular peninsula bridges Africa and Asia, and holds Mount Sinai and St Catherine's Monastery, one of the oldest in the world.
Places in Egypt.Aswan: The southern Nile city sits at the first cataract, and its pink granite was used for obelisks.
Places in Egypt.Petra: A trap. This rose-red city carved into the cliffs is in Jordan, built by the Nabataeans, not in Egypt.
Places in Egypt.Timbuktu: Mali's desert city was a medieval center of learning and trade, with thousands of manuscripts still preserved there.
Places in Egypt.Persepolis: The ceremonial capital of the Persian Empire in Iran was burned by Alexander the Great in 330 BC.
Places in Egypt.Carthage: This ancient Phoenician city, in modern Tunisia, rivaled Rome until Rome destroyed it in 146 BC.
Places in Egypt.Marrakesh: Morocco's red city is known for its Jemaa el-Fnaa square, and it is a long way from the Nile.
Places in Egypt.Dead Sea: Egypt does not border it. Its shore, shared by Jordan, Israel and the West Bank, is the lowest dry land on Earth.
Places in Egypt.Babylon: The Mesopotamian city in Iraq is linked to the legendary Hanging Gardens, and Hammurabi once ruled from it.
Places in Egypt.Casablanca: Morocco's largest city has a Spanish name meaning white house, and the Hassan II Mosque rises over the Atlantic.
Places in Egypt.Mecca: Saudi Arabia's holy city, birthplace of Muhammad, draws millions of pilgrims to the Kaaba for the annual Hajj.
Places in Egypt.Damascus: Syria's capital is often claimed as one of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities.
Places in Egypt.Baghdad: Founded in AD 762 as a round city, it became the heart of the Abbasid Islamic Golden Age, and lies in Iraq.
Places in Egypt.Tunis: Tunisia's capital sits near the ruins of ancient Carthage, and it is nowhere near Egypt.
Places in Egypt.Tripoli: The name is Greek for three cities. It is Libya's capital, on the Mediterranean west of Egypt.

Found in Germany.Brandenburg Gate: Berlin's neoclassical gate was inspired by Athens' Propylaea and once stood in the shadow of the Wall.
Found in Germany.Black Forest: A dense, wooded Baden-Württemberg range known for cuckoo clocks, and for the cherry-laced cake named after it.

Found in Germany.Rügen: Germany's largest island, famed for its white chalk cliffs that inspired Caspar David Friedrich.

Famous city squares.Red Square: Moscow's famous plaza is bordered by the Kremlin and St. Basil's Cathedral, and the name comes from an old Russian word for beautiful, not the color.
Famous city squares.Trafalgar Square: London's square commemorates Nelson's 1805 naval victory, and its fourth plinth displays rotating contemporary artworks.
Famous city squares.Plaza Mayor: Madrid's arcaded main square dates to the early 1600s, and it has hosted bullfights, markets and royal celebrations.
Famous city squares.Grand Place: Brussels' ornate guildhall square is a UNESCO site, and every two years it is carpeted with a flower display of about a million begonias.
Famous city squares.Wenceslas Square: Prague's boulevard-like square saw the 1989 Velvet Revolution rallies, and it is named after the patron saint of Bohemia.
Famous city squares.Piazza Navona: Rome's oval piazza follows the shape of an ancient Roman stadium, and Bernini's Fountain of the Four Rivers stands at its center.
Famous city squares.Zócalo: Mexico City's main square sits atop the Aztec capital of Tenochtitlan, and it is one of the largest city squares in the world.
Famous city squares.Jemaa el-Fnaa: Marrakech's marketplace fills at dusk with storytellers, musicians and food stalls, and it is a UNESCO intangible heritage space.
Famous city squares.Place de la Concorde: Paris' biggest square held the guillotine during the Revolution, and now has an Egyptian obelisk about 3,000 years old.
Famous city squares.Dam Square: Amsterdam's central square is named for the dam on the Amstel River that founded the city, and the Royal Palace stands on it.
Famous city squares.Plaza de Mayo: Buenos Aires' main plaza, where the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo have marched since 1977 to demand news of the disappeared.
Famous city squares.Central Park: New York's park is 843 acres of designed landscape, not a paved square, and it opened in the 1850s.
Famous city squares.Hyde Park: London's royal park has Speakers' Corner, where anyone can make a speech, but it is a park rather than a square.
Famous city squares.Champs-Élysées: A grand avenue in Paris, running from the Place de la Concorde to the Arc de Triomphe, and not a square.
Famous city squares.La Rambla: Barcelona's tree-lined pedestrian street runs from the city center to the harbor, and it is a promenade, not a square.
Famous city squares.Broadway: The long avenue crosses Manhattan from end to end, and the theater district around it gives it fame; it is a street.
Famous city squares.Golden Gate Park: San Francisco's park is bigger than Central Park, and it is a park, not a square.
Famous city squares.Tivoli Gardens: Copenhagen's amusement park opened in 1843 and is one of the oldest in the world, and it is a garden, not a square.
Famous city squares.Vondelpark: Amsterdam's biggest city park is named after the poet Joost van den Vondel, and it is a park rather than a square.
Famous city squares.Englischer Garten: Munich's large park has a beer garden and surfers riding a standing wave on the Eisbach stream.
Famous city squares.Boboli Gardens: Florence's Renaissance gardens behind the Pitti Palace are a showcase of Italian garden design, not a city square.
Famous city squares.Retiro Park: Madrid's big green park began as royal grounds and has a glass Crystal Palace, but it is a park.
Famous city squares.Fifth Avenue: Manhattan's famous shopping street divides the city's east from its west, and it is an avenue, not a square.

National capitals in Oceania.Suva: Fiji's capital on Viti Levu is among the largest cities in the Pacific islands and a regional hub for shipping and universities.

National capitals in Oceania.Apia: Robert Louis Stevenson spent his last years near Samoa's capital and is buried on nearby Mount Vaea overlooking the sea.
National capitals in Oceania.Nuku'alofa: Tonga's capital belongs to a kingdom that was never fully colonized and still has a monarch; it is the Pacific's only kingdom of its kind.
National capitals in Oceania.Port Vila: Vanuatu's capital on Efate was once run by Britain and France jointly as the New Hebrides, under a unique 'condominium' that ended in 1980.
National capitals in Oceania.Honiara: Capital of the Solomon Islands, on Guadalcanal, where a major World War II battle in 1942 and 1943 was fought around Henderson Field.
National capitals in Oceania.Majuro: The Marshall Islands' capital is a narrow coral atoll only a few meters above sea level, which makes it a symbol of climate-change risk.
National capitals in Oceania.Palikir: The Federated States of Micronesia is governed from this tiny village on Pohnpei, one of the smallest capitals on Earth.
National capitals in Oceania.Sydney: Australia's biggest city and home of the Opera House, but never the national capital; that is Canberra.
National capitals in Oceania.Auckland: New Zealand's largest city was actually the capital until 1865, when government moved south to Wellington.
National capitals in Oceania.Melbourne: It served as Australia's temporary capital from 1901 to 1927 while Canberra was being built, but it isn't one now.
National capitals in Oceania.Nadi: Nadi is Fiji's main international airport town, not the capital; that role belongs to Suva.
National capitals in Oceania.Honolulu: Honolulu is the capital of the US state of Hawaii, not of an independent country.
National capitals in Oceania.Papeete: Papeete is the capital of French Polynesia, an overseas collectivity of France, so it isn't a sovereign nation's capital.
National capitals in Oceania.Nouméa: Nouméa is the capital of New Caledonia, a French territory with a nickel-mining economy, so it doesn't count as a national capital.
National capitals in Oceania.Hagåtña: Hagåtña is the capital of Guam, a US territory, and one of the smallest capitals under American flag.
National capitals in Oceania.Christchurch: Christchurch is the South Island's largest city, rebuilt after the damaging 2011 earthquake, but it is not New Zealand's capital.
National capitals in Oceania.Lae: Lae is Papua New Guinea's second city and main cargo port, and it's the end of the Highlands Highway, but not the capital.
National capitals in Oceania.Brisbane: Brisbane is the capital of Queensland, a state, not of Australia.
National capitals in Oceania.Pago Pago: Pago Pago is the capital of American Samoa, a US territory, with one of the Pacific's deepest natural harbors.
National capitals in Oceania.Queenstown: The adventure-sports town in New Zealand, where commercial bungee jumping began off the Kawarau Bridge in 1988, is no capital.
National capitals in Oceania.Perth: Perth is often called the most isolated major city in the world, but it is only a state capital, not a national one.

Igneous rocks.Granite: A coarse rock formed from slowly cooled magma deep underground. Its large visible crystals, mainly quartz and feldspar, result from that slow cooling.
Igneous rocks.Basalt: The most common volcanic rock on Earth, it forms most of the ocean floor. Cooling lava can fracture into hexagonal columns, as at the Giant's Causeway.
Igneous rocks.Obsidian: A natural volcanic glass formed when lava cools too fast to crystallize. Stone Age people made blades from it that are sharper than steel scalpels.
Igneous rocks.Pumice: Lava frothed with gas bubbles then cooled, so full of holes it can float on water. Rafts of it have drifted across oceans for years.
Igneous rocks.Gabbro: The coarse-grained cousin of basalt, formed when the same magma cools slowly underground. Much of the deep oceanic crust is gabbro.
Igneous rocks.Andesite: A volcanic rock named for the Andes, where it is common. It is typical of volcanoes above subduction zones.
Igneous rocks.Rhyolite: The fast-cooled, volcanic twin of granite, with the same chemistry. Yellowstone's huge eruptions left thick layers of it.
Igneous rocks.Diorite: A speckled black-and-white intrusive rock, between granite and gabbro. Ancient Mesopotamians carved statues and the Code of Hammurabi stele from diorite.
Igneous rocks.Scoria: A dark, dotted, volcanic rock full of gas bubbles, heavier than pumice. It is used in barbecue grills and landscaping.
Igneous rocks.Marble: A trap: marble is metamorphic, made when limestone is baked and squeezed. Its crystals interlock, giving a glow that sculptors love.
Igneous rocks.Slate: A trap: it's metamorphic, formed from shale pressed under heat. It splits cleanly into sheets.
Igneous rocks.Limestone: A trap: it is sedimentary, built from shells and coral over millions of years. It sometimes contains fossils.
Igneous rocks.Sandstone: A trap: sedimentary, formed from cemented sand grains. Its layers often show ancient dunes or riverbeds.
Igneous rocks.Shale: A trap: sedimentary, made of compacted mud. It splits into thin layers and often traps fossils.
Igneous rocks.Chalk: A trap: sedimentary, built from the skeletons of microscopic algae called coccolithophores.
Igneous rocks.Quartzite: A trap: it's metamorphic, formed when sandstone is heated and squeezed until the grains fuse. It's extremely hard.
Igneous rocks.Gneiss: A trap: a banded metamorphic rock, produced when granite or other rock is heated and squashed. Some gneiss is over 3 billion years old.
Igneous rocks.Schist: A trap: metamorphic, with a sparkly, flaky texture from aligned mica crystals. Manhattan's skyscrapers stand on bedrock of it.
Igneous rocks.Coal: A trap: it is sedimentary, formed from compressed ancient plants over hundreds of millions of years, not from fire or magma.
Igneous rocks.Conglomerate: A trap: it's sedimentary, with rounded pebbles cemented together like a stone pudding.
Igneous rocks.Flint: A trap: a sedimentary rock, often found inside chalk. It breaks with sharp edges and sparks when struck with steel.
Igneous rocks.Travertine: A trap: sedimentary, deposited by mineral-rich springs. The Colosseum in Rome was built largely from it.
Igneous rocks.Mudstone: A trap: sedimentary, formed from hardened mud and clay. It is much like shale but doesn't split into layers.
Igneous rocks.Soapstone: A trap: a soft, metamorphic rock rich in talc, so it feels soapy. It holds heat well and has been used for stoves and carvings.

Forms of energy.Kinetic: The energy of motion grows with the square of speed, so doubling a car's speed quadruples the energy to shed when braking.
Forms of energy.Potential: Stored energy of position; a boulder on a cliff holds it, and a dam's reservoir stores it to be turned into electricity.
Forms of energy.Thermal: Heat is just the jostling of atoms; at absolute zero, about minus 273 degrees C, that motion nearly stops.
Forms of energy.Chemical: Stored in molecular bonds; your body releases it from food, and a gram of fat holds more than twice that of a gram of sugar.
Forms of energy.Nuclear: Locked in the atom's core; Einstein's E=mc2 explains why a tiny bit of mass converts to enormous energy.
Forms of energy.Electrical: Energy of moving charge; your nerves run on tiny electrical signals, and a single lightning bolt carries billions of joules.
Forms of energy.Sound: A form of mechanical energy in vibrating air; it needs a medium, so in space nobody can hear you scream.
Forms of energy.Light: A form of radiant energy that powers nearly all life; sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach Earth.
Forms of energy.Elastic: Energy stored in a stretched or squeezed object, like a bowstring or a spring, ready to snap back.
Forms of energy.Gravitational: Stored energy in a lifted object; roller coasters trade it for speed as they drop from the first big hill.
Forms of energy.Radiant: Energy that travels as electromagnetic waves, needing no medium, which is how the Sun's warmth crosses empty space.
Forms of energy.Velocity: A trap: velocity is speed with direction. It is a measurement of motion, though kinetic energy depends on it.
Forms of energy.Mass: A trap: how much matter an object has. It is not energy, though E=mc2 links the two.
Forms of energy.Friction: A trap: a force, not an energy form; it turns motion into heat, which is why rubbing your hands warms them.
Forms of energy.Momentum: A trap: mass times velocity, a quantity that is conserved in collisions, unlike energy, which can change forms.
Forms of energy.Acceleration: A trap: the rate velocity changes, and not energy. Gravity near Earth's surface accelerates things by about 9.8 m/s per second.
Forms of energy.Density: A trap: mass per unit volume. It decides whether things sink or float, but it is no kind of energy.
Forms of energy.Torque: A trap: a twisting force, measured in newton-meters, the same unit as energy, which makes people confuse them.
Forms of energy.Pressure: A trap: force per area, not energy form, though a pressurized gas can store energy.
Forms of energy.Inertia: A trap: a property of matter that resists changes in motion, not energy; Newton's first law describes it.
Forms of energy.Volume: A trap: how much space something takes up. Nothing to do with energy, though a loud sound carries more.
Forms of energy.Weight: A trap: the pull of gravity on mass, a force. Your weight on the Moon is about a sixth of Earth's.
Forms of energy.Temperature: A trap: a measure of average particle motion, not the energy itself; a bathtub of warm water holds more heat than a hot spark.
Forms of energy.Speed: A trap: just how fast something moves; it's a measurement, not an energy type, though kinetic energy depends on it.

Things a magnet will pick up.Iron nail: Iron is one of only a few magnetic metals, and a nail can even become a temporary magnet when rubbed along one.
Things a magnet will pick up.Paperclip: Most are steel, which is mostly iron, so magnets cling to them, and a paperclip chain can hang from a magnet.
Things a magnet will pick up.Iron filings: These tiny bits of iron line up along magnetic field lines, which is the classic way to make the field visible.
Things a magnet will pick up.Steel wool: Made of fine steel strands, so a magnet picks it up, and it can even burn if you touch it to a battery.
Things a magnet will pick up.Safety pin: Usually steel, so magnetic, though some are brass-plated and may not stick as well.
Things a magnet will pick up.Thumbtack: Often steel with a coating, so it can be picked up, though a few are brass and won't be.
Things a magnet will pick up.Bobby pin: Typically steel with a coating, so a magnet snags it right away.
Things a magnet will pick up.Staple: Made of thin steel wire, so a magnet will grab them from a desk drawer.
Things a magnet will pick up.Sewing needle: Steel needles are easily magnetized, which is how early sailors made compass needles floating in water.
Things a magnet will pick up.Ball bearing: Chrome steel balls reduce friction in machines, and a magnet pulls them readily.
Things a magnet will pick up.Aluminum can: A trap: aluminum isn't magnetic, which is how recycling plants separate it from steel cans.
Things a magnet will pick up.Copper wire: A trap: not magnetic itself, though a moving magnet near copper creates currents that slow the magnet down.
Things a magnet will pick up.Gold ring: A trap: gold isn't magnetic, which is one handy test for fakes; if a magnet sticks, it's not pure gold.
Things a magnet will pick up.Silver spoon: A trap: silver isn't magnetic, though it's strongly diamagnetic, pushing very slightly away from a magnet.
Things a magnet will pick up.Brass key: A trap: brass is copper and zinc, with no iron, so a magnet ignores it.
Things a magnet will pick up.Plastic button: A trap: plastic has no magnetic metals, so magnets pass right through it.
Things a magnet will pick up.Rubber band: A trap: rubber is non-metallic and unaffected by magnets.
Things a magnet will pick up.Glass marble: A trap: glass is not magnetic, though it feels heavy and solid like a bearing.
Things a magnet will pick up.Wooden pencil: A trap: wood and graphite don't respond to magnets, so the pencil stays put.
Things a magnet will pick up.Tin foil: A trap: aluminum foil, nowadays, is not magnetic, and old real tin foil wasn't either.
Things a magnet will pick up.Lead weight: A trap: lead is heavy but not magnetic, with no pull at all.
Things a magnet will pick up.Feather: A trap: feathers are made of keratin, not magnetic metal.
Things a magnet will pick up.Cork: A trap: it is plant bark, which is non-magnetic and floats.
Things a magnet will pick up.Sugar cube: A trap: sugar is organic, so it has no magnetic response at all.

Units of energy.Joule: The SI unit of energy, and lifting an apple one meter takes about one; a food Calorie is about 4,184 joules.
Units of energy.Calorie: The small calorie raises one gram of water by one degree C, and food Calories on labels are 1,000 of them.
Units of energy.Kilowatt-hour: What your electricity bill measures; one equals 3.6 million joules, about running a 1,000-watt heater for an hour.
Units of energy.Electronvolt: The energy an electron gains across one volt, and particle physicists use it because joules are far too large for atoms.
Units of energy.BTU: The British thermal unit is the heat to warm a pound of water one degree Fahrenheit, and it rates air conditioners and heaters.
Units of energy.Erg: A tiny unit from the old CGS system, one ten-millionth of a joule, still used by astronomers for stars' energy.
Units of energy.Therm: 100,000 BTU, used on British and US gas bills to measure how much heat gas supplies.
Units of energy.Kilocalorie: The scientific name for the food Calorie; what labels call calories are really kilocalories.
Units of energy.Foot-pound: Energy from lifting one pound one foot, about 1.36 joules, and it's still used to rate firearms and torque wrenches.
Units of energy.Watt: A trap: a measure of power, which is energy per time; one watt is one joule per second.
Units of energy.Volt: A trap: measures electric potential, not energy; energy needs charge multiplied by voltage.
Units of energy.Ampere: A trap: the unit of electric current, which is charge flowing each second, not energy.
Units of energy.Newton: A trap: a unit of force, named for Isaac Newton, and about the weight of a small apple.
Units of energy.Horsepower: A trap: a unit of power, invented by James Watt to sell steam engines by comparison with horses, about 746 watts.
Units of energy.Ohm: A trap: a unit of electrical resistance, named for Georg Ohm.
Units of energy.Pascal: A trap: a unit of pressure, equal to one newton per square meter, named for Blaise Pascal.
Units of energy.Hertz: A trap: a unit of frequency, one cycle per second, named for Heinrich Hertz, who produced radio waves in 1887.
Units of energy.Kelvin: A trap: a temperature unit starting at absolute zero, not energy, though temperature relates to particle energy.
Units of energy.Tesla: A trap: a unit of magnetic field strength, named after Nikola Tesla; an MRI scanner uses fields of one to three.
Units of energy.Coulomb: A trap: the unit of electric charge, about six quintillion electrons' worth.
Units of energy.Lumen: A trap: it measures the brightness of a light source, as light output, and not energy.
Units of energy.Decibel: A trap: a logarithmic scale for sound level, not an energy unit, where adding 10 dB means ten times the power.
Units of energy.Knot: A trap: a speed at sea, one nautical mile per hour, so it has nothing to do with energy.
Units of energy.Farad: A trap: a unit of electrical capacitance, named after Michael Faraday, and a full farad is huge in practice.

Japanese anime series.Dragon Ball: Akira Toriyama began it in 1984, loosely inspired by the Chinese novel Journey to the West.
Japanese anime series.Sailor Moon: Naoko Takeuchi's 1990s magical-girl series gave each Sailor Guardian a planet-based theme.
Japanese anime series.Death Note: A notebook that kills whoever's name is written in it. The death god Ryuk is famously obsessed with apples.
Japanese anime series.Attack on Titan: Hajime Isayama's manga ran from 2009 to 2021, and the anime's final part concluded in 2023.
Japanese anime series.Pokemon: The anime began in 1997. Ash stayed ten years old for about 25 years before finally winning a world title in 2022.
Japanese anime series.Demon Slayer: Its 2020 film Mugen Train became the highest-grossing Japanese film ever released at the time.
Japanese anime series.Cowboy Bebop: A 1998 space-bounty-hunter series scored by Yoko Kanno, with a jazz-heavy soundtrack.

Famous guitarists.Stevie Ray Vaughan: The Texas bluesman died in a helicopter crash in 1990 at age 35.

Famous guitarists.Roger Daltrey: The Who's singer. The guitarist was Pete Townshend.
Famous guitarists.Charlie Watts: The Rolling Stones' drummer for nearly 60 years was a jazz fan at heart, and he kept time rather than playing guitar.
Famous guitarists.Lionel Richie: The Commodores' singer and songwriter, behind Three Times a Lady.

Pokemon types.Fire: Charmander's type is strong against Grass, Bug, Ice and Steel, but weak to Water, Rock and Ground.
Pokemon types.Water: Squirtle's type is the most common in the games, with more Pokemon than any other; it's strong against Fire, Ground and Rock.
Pokemon types.Grass: Bulbasaur's type, which is weak to Fire, Ice, Poison, Flying and Bug, many more weaknesses than most types.
Pokemon types.Electric: Pikachu's type is super effective against Water and Flying, but Ground types are completely immune to it.
Pokemon types.Psychic: This type was famously overpowered in the original games, partly because of a bug that left Ghost moves unable to hit it.
Pokemon types.Ghost: Normal and Fighting moves can't affect them, which is why they made Gengar so tough to deal with.
Pokemon types.Dragon: Introduced in the first games with few members, it's weak only to Ice, Dragon and Fairy.
Pokemon types.Fairy: Added in 2013's Pokemon X and Y, the first new type since 2000, mainly to weaken Dragons.
Pokemon types.Steel: Introduced in Gold and Silver, it resists more types than any other, having 10 resistances.
Pokemon types.Dark: Also added in Gold and Silver, in 1999, to counter the overpowered Psychic type.
Pokemon types.Ice: Weak to many types, including Fire and Fighting, but its attacks hit Dragon, Flying, Grass and Ground hard.
Pokemon types.Bug: Caterpie and Weedle were among the first Pokemon players met; the type is inspired by creator Satoshi Tajiri's childhood insect collecting.
Pokemon types.Rock: Geodude, Onix and Aerodactyl are Rock types; they're weak to many types, including Water and Grass.
Pokemon types.Poison: Super effective against Grass and Fairy; Poison types can't be poisoned, and Steel types are immune to it.
Pokemon types.Light: Not a Pokemon type, though plenty of moves shine; the 18 types include Fairy and Dark instead.
Pokemon types.Sound: Sound is a move category, like Hyper Voice, and not a type; those moves are mostly Normal-type.
Pokemon types.Wind: There's no Wind type; air-themed Pokemon usually are Flying, which does include moves like Gust.
Pokemon types.Metal: The type is called Steel; Metal is not a Pokemon type, even though many Steel Pokemon like Magnemite look metallic.
Pokemon types.Wood: No Wood type exists; trees and plants fall under Grass.
Pokemon types.Earth: The earth-based type is Ground; Rock is separate.
Pokemon types.Air: Pokemon use Flying for air creatures; there is no Air type.
Pokemon types.Lightning: The type is called Electric; 'Lightning' is the name used in the Pokemon Trading Card Game.
Pokemon types.Shadow: Shadow Pokemon exist in the Colosseum games and Pokemon Go, but they're a state, not a type.
Pokemon types.Magic: A trap: Magic isn't a type; magical effects mostly come under Psychic or Fairy.

Kids' games that need a ball.Dodgeball: Players throw soft balls to knock opponents out, and the name of the game is also a Ben Stiller film from 2004.
Kids' games that need a ball.Kickball: Kids kick a rubber ball and run bases, and it was invented in 1917 by a Cincinnati educator, who called it Kick Baseball.
Kids' games that need a ball.Four square: Four players in a grid of squares bounce a ball between them, and it's a staple of school playgrounds.
Kids' games that need a ball.Tetherball: A ball on a rope around a pole is hit in opposite directions, and the player who wraps the rope fully wins.
Kids' games that need a ball.Catch: Throwing a ball back and forth has been called the simplest game there is, and parents can use it to teach hand-eye coordination.
Kids' games that need a ball.Keep away: Players toss a ball over a person in the middle trying to grab it, a game also called monkey in the middle.
Kids' games that need a ball.Wall ball: A ball is thrown against a wall, and players must catch it, so you only need a wall and a ball.
Kids' games that need a ball.Monkey in the middle: The player in the middle tries to intercept the ball, and it's called piggy in the middle in Britain.
Kids' games that need a ball.Jacks: Players bounce a small ball, then pick up metal pieces before it bounces again, and the game goes back to ancient Greece with knucklebones.
Kids' games that need a ball.Spud: Players number themselves and scatter when a ball is thrown, and the caller shouts a number and everyone dashes away.
Kids' games that need a ball.Kick the can: A can replaces the ball, so no ball is needed, and the game is a mix of hide and seek and tag.
Kids' games that need a ball.Hopscotch: Chalked squares to hop through are a game thought to go back to Roman times, when kids marked courts in the dust of roads.
Kids' games that need a ball.Tag: A chasing game that needs only people, and there are many variations around the world.
Kids' games that need a ball.Red Rover: Two lines of children call over a runner who tries to break their linked arms, with no ball.
Kids' games that need a ball.Simon Says: Players obey commands only if prefaced by the phrase, and it trains listening, not ball skills.
Kids' games that need a ball.Duck Duck Goose: Children sit in a circle and a tagger picks one, which is a game that needs no ball.
Kids' games that need a ball.Leapfrog: One player bends over and another vaults over, so it needs only bodies.
Kids' games that need a ball.Hide and seek: A seeker counts while the others hide, so no equipment is needed.
Kids' games that need a ball.Musical chairs: Kids walk around chairs until the music stops and then scramble for a seat, so the game needs no ball.
Kids' games that need a ball.Tug of war: Two teams pull on a rope, and it was once an Olympic event, from 1900 to 1920.
Kids' games that need a ball.Jump rope: Skipping rope can be a fitness tool, and boxers use it to improve footwork, but it requires a rope, not a ball.
Kids' games that need a ball.Freeze tag: Taggers freeze players until a friend unfreezes them, which makes it a chase game without equipment.
Kids' games that need a ball.Sardines: One person hides and the others squeeze in as they find them, a reverse hide and seek that needs no ball.
Kids' games that need a ball.Statues: Players freeze in place when the music stops, so no ball is needed.

Sports whose names end in 'ball'.Football: The oldest of the family; the game takes its name from being played on foot rather than horseback. Americans call it soccer.
Sports whose names end in 'ball'.Baseball: Baseball ends in 'ball' and was reportedly refined into its modern form in 19th-century America. Myths about Abner Doubleday inventing it are widely doubted.
Sports whose names end in 'ball'.Basketball: James Naismith invented basketball in 1891, first using peach baskets with the bottoms still in, so after each score someone had to fetch the ball.
Sports whose names end in 'ball'.Volleyball: Volleyball was originally called mintonette, created in 1895 by William Morgan in Massachusetts.
Sports whose names end in 'ball'.Netball: Netball grew out of early basketball in Britain and is especially popular in Commonwealth countries; players can't run with the ball.
Sports whose names end in 'ball'.Handball: Olympic team handball, played with seven per side, is fast and high scoring, and a Danish teacher codified it in the early 1900s.
Sports whose names end in 'ball'.Softball: Softball began in 1887 as an indoor game in Chicago, played with a boxing glove and a broomstick. The ball isn't actually soft.
Sports whose names end in 'ball'.Dodgeball: Dodgeball is a well-known school game, but organized leagues exist worldwide, and the sport has its own world championship.
Sports whose names end in 'ball'.Kickball: Kickball resembles baseball, but the pitcher rolls a big rubber ball and the batter kicks it.
Sports whose names end in 'ball'.Paintball: Paintball's first game was played in New Hampshire in 1981 by 12 players. The 'balls' are gelatin capsules filled with dye.
Sports whose names end in 'ball'.Racquetball: Racquetball is played in an enclosed court with a hollow rubber ball, and it was invented in 1950 by Joe Sobek in Connecticut.
Sports whose names end in 'ball'.Floorball: Floorball is a fast indoor hockey game with a plastic ball full of holes. It's especially big in Sweden and Finland.
Sports whose names end in 'ball'.Pickleball: Pickleball mixes tennis, badminton and ping pong and uses a plastic ball with holes. It's among America's fastest growing sports.
Sports whose names end in 'ball'.Bowling: Bowling uses a ball, but the name doesn't end with it; it ends in 'ing'. Ten-pin bowling is traced to medieval Germany, perhaps earlier.
Sports whose names end in 'ball'.Squash: Squash is a racquet sport played with a small rubber ball, but the name doesn't end in ball. It's also a vegetable.
Sports whose names end in 'ball'.Tennis: Tennis has a ball but the name doesn't end in it. It evolved from jeu de paume, played by French monks, sometimes using the palm.
Sports whose names end in 'ball'.Golf: Golf's ball is tiny, with 300 or more dimples, but its name doesn't say so.
Sports whose names end in 'ball'.Cricket: Cricket is played with a ball, but the name has nothing to do with it; it may come from an old word for a stick.
Sports whose names end in 'ball'.Lacrosse: Lacrosse started as Native American games called baggataway, and the French name refers to the stick's shape.
Sports whose names end in 'ball'.Croquet: Croquet is played with hoops and mallets, not a ball in the name. It was an Olympic sport only in 1900, in Paris, with very few entrants.
Sports whose names end in 'ball'.Rugby: Rugby is named for Rugby School in England. The ball is oval, but the name doesn't end in 'ball'.
Sports whose names end in 'ball'.Polo: Polo is among the oldest team sports, first played in Persia. It uses a ball but the name has no 'ball' ending.
Sports whose names end in 'ball'.Bocce: Bocce is an Italian lawn game that is played with balls, but the name ends in 'e'.
Sports whose names end in 'ball'.Billiards: Billiards uses balls but the word doesn't end with 'ball'. It's been played since the 15th century.

The nine Muses.Calliope: The Muse of epic poetry, considered the leader of the nine. She is the mother of Orpheus in many tellings.
The nine Muses.Clio: The Muse of history, often shown with a scroll. Her name means "to make famous."
The nine Muses.Erato: The Muse of love poetry, often with a lyre. Her name comes from the Greek for "lovely."
The nine Muses.Euterpe: The Muse of music and lyric poetry, usually shown with a flute. Her name means "giver of much delight."
The nine Muses.Melpomene: The Muse of tragedy, shown with a tragic mask. Her name means "the singer," though her art later became the grimmest in drama.
The nine Muses.Polyhymnia: The Muse of sacred hymns and eloquence, often pictured veiled and pensive. Her name means "many hymns."
The nine Muses.Terpsichore: The Muse of dance, whose name gives us the adjective "terpsichorean," which means "relating to dancing."
The nine Muses.Thalia: The Muse of comedy, usually holding a comic mask. A different Thalia was one of the three Graces.
The nine Muses.Urania: The Muse of astronomy, often shown with a globe and compass. The planet Uranus shares the root of her name.
The nine Muses.Athena: A goddess of wisdom and crafts, often a patron of the arts and learning, but not one of the Muses.
The nine Muses.Artemis: Goddess of the hunt and the moon, twin of Apollo. She is Olympian and not a Muse.
The nine Muses.Aphrodite: The goddess of love and beauty, said to be born from sea foam. She is Olympian, not a Muse.
The nine Muses.Hera: Queen of the gods and goddess of marriage. She is Zeus's wife, not his daughter, so not a Muse.
The nine Muses.Persephone: Queen of the underworld, who spends part of the year there. A goddess tied to seasons, not a Muse.
The nine Muses.Pandora: The first woman, whose jar (actually a large jar, not a box) released misfortunes. She isn't a Muse.
The nine Muses.Medusa: The Gorgon whose gaze turned people to stone, a monster with no link to the Muses.
The nine Muses.Psyche: A mortal princess who became a goddess of the soul after trials set by Aphrodite. Her name means "soul" or "breath."
The nine Muses.Helen: The famed beauty whose abduction led to the Trojan War. A mortal woman, not a Muse.
The nine Muses.Penelope: Odysseus's patient wife, who put off suitors for years by unpicking her weaving each night.
The nine Muses.Ariadne: The Cretan princess who gave Theseus the thread to escape the Labyrinth. A princess, not a Muse.
The nine Muses.Cassandra: A Trojan princess cursed to speak true prophecies that no one believed. Not one of the Muses.
The nine Muses.Echo: A nymph who could only repeat others' words. She is a nymph, not one of the nine Muses.
The nine Muses.Daphne: A nymph who turned into a laurel tree to escape Apollo. Laurel wreaths for poets and victors remember her.
The nine Muses.Iris: The goddess of the rainbow and a messenger of the gods. She's a divine messenger, not a Muse.

Named after a god (months, days, planets.January: From Janus, Roman god of doors and beginnings, who had two faces looking back and ahead. A fitting patron for the start of the year.
Named after a god (months, days, planets.March: Named for Mars, Roman god of war. It was the first month of the early Roman calendar, which is when campaigning season began.
Named after a god (months, days, planets.Tuesday: Tiw's day, after the Norse and Germanic war god Týr. Romance languages kept Mars: mardi in French, martes in Spanish.
Named after a god (months, days, planets.Wednesday: Woden's day, after the chief Germanic god, who is Odin. Romans linked him with Mercury, which is why French says mercredi.
Named after a god (months, days, planets.Thursday: Thor's day, honouring the thunder god. Latin called it Jupiter's day, and Thor was the Germanic match for Jupiter.
Named after a god (months, days, planets.Friday: Frigg's day, named for Odin's wife (or possibly Freyja). The Romans' version was Venus, so French says vendredi.
Named after a god (months, days, planets.Saturday: The only English weekday still named for a Roman god. It is Saturn's day, after the god of harvest and time.
Named after a god (months, days, planets.Mercury: The smallest planet, named for the Roman messenger god because it zips around the Sun in just 88 days.
Named after a god (months, days, planets.Venus: The hottest planet, with a surface near 465 degrees Celsius thanks to a runaway greenhouse effect. It is named for the Roman goddess of love.
Named after a god (months, days, planets.Jupiter: The largest planet, named for the king of the Roman gods. Its Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth.
Named after a god (months, days, planets.Neptune: Named for the Roman sea god. Found in 1846 by using maths to predict its position from Uranus's wobble, before anyone looked through a telescope.
Named after a god (months, days, planets.Pluto: Named after the Roman god of the underworld in 1930 by 11-year-old Venetia Burney. It was reclassified a dwarf planet in 2006.
Named after a god (months, days, planets.Uranus: The odd one out: named for the Greek sky god Ouranos, not a Roman one. It also spins on its side, tilted by about 98 degrees.
Named after a god (months, days, planets.Earth: Almost the only planet not named for a god. Its name comes from Old English and Germanic words for ground, so it is a trap here.
Named after a god (months, days, planets.July: Named for Julius Caesar, a man, not a god. The Senate renamed it Julius in his honour after his death. It is the month that does not fit.
Named after a god (months, days, planets.August: Named for Emperor Augustus, who was a man, even if later deified. It used to be called Sextilis, the sixth month.
Named after a god (months, days, planets.September: Simply "seventh month" in Latin, though it is now ninth. The numbered names (Sept, Oct, Nov, Dec) refer to the old ten-month calendar.
Named after a god (months, days, planets.October: Means "eighth month" in Latin, a leftover from when March began the year. It was never named for a deity.
Named after a god (months, days, planets.November: Latin for "ninth month". It carries a number, not a god, and fell out of step when January and February were added to the start.
Named after a god (months, days, planets.December: The "tenth month" of the old Roman year, which is why it now sits twelfth. A number, not a deity.
Named after a god (months, days, planets.Moon: A plain English word from Old English mona. Most other languages use similar names, though the Roman moon goddess Luna gives us "lunar".
Named after a god (months, days, planets.Milky Way: Our galaxy, named for its milky band of stars. The Greeks said it was milk spilled by Hera, and "galaxy" itself comes from the Greek for milk.
Named after a god (months, days, planets.Big Dipper: An asterism, not a god. It lies inside the constellation Ursa Major, the Great Bear, and its end stars point to Polaris.
Named after a god (months, days, planets.Halley's Comet: Named for Edmond Halley, who worked out in 1705 that comets seen in 1531, 1607 and 1682 were one object. It returns about every 76 years.

Battles of World War II.Stalingrad: The 1942 to 1943 battle destroyed Germany's Sixth Army and turned the Eastern Front, among the bloodiest battles in history.
Battles of World War II.Midway: In June 1942 US forces sank four Japanese carriers, helped by codebreakers who had read Japan's plans.
Battles of World War II.El Alamein: The 1942 victory in Egypt prompted Churchill to say it was not the end, but the end of the beginning.
Battles of World War II.Kursk: The 1943 clash, one of history's largest tank battles, was Germany's last major offensive in the east.
Battles of World War II.Iwo Jima: The February 1945 battle produced the famous photograph of Marines raising a flag on Mount Suribachi.
Battles of World War II.Okinawa: The 1945 battle was the Pacific war's largest amphibious landing, and a big factor in thinking about invading Japan.
Battles of World War II.Battle of Britain: In 1940 the RAF held off the Luftwaffe, and Churchill said never was so much owed by so many to so few.
Battles of World War II.Battle of the Bulge: Germany's last big offensive in the west, in December 1944, was named for the salient it punched in the Allied line.
Battles of World War II.Guadalcanal: The 1942 to 1943 campaign was the Allies' first major offensive against Japan.
Battles of World War II.Monte Cassino: The 1944 fight ended after the ancient abbey was bombed and Polish troops captured the ruins.
Battles of World War II.Dunkirk: In 1940 more than 330,000 Allied troops were evacuated, aided by hundreds of civilian little ships.
Battles of World War II.Somme: A World War I battle of 1916, when British forces suffered roughly 57,000 casualties on the first day alone.
Battles of World War II.Verdun: A World War I battle of 1916 lasting about ten months, still a symbol of French resistance.
Battles of World War II.Gallipoli: A World War I campaign of 1915 that shaped national identity in Australia and New Zealand.
Battles of World War II.Ypres: A World War I battle site in Belgium, where chlorine gas was first used on a large scale in 1915.
Battles of World War II.Passchendaele: The 1917 World War I battle became a symbol of mud and slaughter on the Western Front.
Battles of World War II.Marne: A World War I clash in 1914 that stopped the German advance on Paris, partly aided by taxis carrying troops.
Battles of World War II.Tannenberg: A 1914 World War I battle where Germany destroyed a Russian army in East Prussia.
Battles of World War II.Waterloo: Napoleon's final defeat in 1815, over a century before World War II and well outside its list of battles.
Battles of World War II.Gettysburg: The 1863 turning point of the American Civil War, fought in Pennsylvania, nearly 80 years before World War II.
Battles of World War II.Hastings: The 1066 battle that brought William the Conqueror to England's throne, almost 900 years before World War II.
Battles of World War II.Trafalgar: Nelson's naval victory of 1805, during the Napoleonic wars, well over a century before World War II.
Battles of World War II.Agincourt: The 1415 English victory over a larger French army in the Hundred Years' War, centuries before World War II.
Battles of World War II.Jutland: The great naval clash of 1916 between British and German fleets belongs to World War I, not World War II.

Linked to Napoleon Bonaparte.Waterloo: Napoleon's final defeat, in Belgium on 18 June 1815, by Wellington and Blucher. The name is now a byword for a decisive downfall.
Linked to Napoleon Bonaparte.Elba: The small Mediterranean island of his first exile in 1814. He ruled it as a mini-kingdom, then escaped after under a year.
Linked to Napoleon Bonaparte.Saint Helena: A remote South Atlantic island where Britain exiled him after Waterloo, and where he died in 1821. It is among the most isolated inhabited places on Earth.
Linked to Napoleon Bonaparte.Josephine: His first wife and empress, whom he divorced in 1810 for lack of an heir. She kept the title and Malmaison, her beloved garden.
Linked to Napoleon Bonaparte.Austerlitz: The 1805 'Battle of the Three Emperors', often called his masterpiece. He beat Russia and Austria on the first anniversary of his coronation.
Linked to Napoleon Bonaparte.Corsica: His birthplace island, which France had acquired from Genoa only a year before he was born in 1769.
Linked to Napoleon Bonaparte.Bicorne hat: The two-cornered hat he wore sideways, unlike officers who wore theirs front to back. It made him easy to spot in battle.
Linked to Napoleon Bonaparte.Napoleonic Code: His 1804 civil code, which swept away feudal privileges and still shapes the legal systems of many countries today.
Linked to Napoleon Bonaparte.Marengo: A 1800 victory in Italy that nearly turned into a defeat until reinforcements arrived late in the day.
Linked to Napoleon Bonaparte.Arc de Triomphe: He commissioned it in 1806 to honour his army, but he never saw it finished. His funeral procession passed beneath it in 1840.
Linked to Napoleon Bonaparte.Louisiana Purchase: He sold the territory to the United States in 1803 for about 15 million dollars, to fund war in Europe. It doubled the size of the US.
Linked to Napoleon Bonaparte.Gettysburg: Trap: a Union victory in the American Civil War in 1863, about half a century after Napoleon's final defeat.
Linked to Napoleon Bonaparte.Hastings: Trap: the 1066 battle in England, where William of Normandy defeated Harold. It happened 700 years earlier.
Linked to Napoleon Bonaparte.Agincourt: Trap: the 1415 English victory over France in the Hundred Years' War, centuries before Napoleon.
Linked to Napoleon Bonaparte.Big Ben: Trap: the bell of London's clock tower, cast in the 1850s, long after Napoleon died in 1821.
Linked to Napoleon Bonaparte.Pearl Harbor: Trap: the 1941 attack on Hawaii that brought America into World War II, over a century after Napoleon.
Linked to Napoleon Bonaparte.Magna Carta: Trap: the 1215 charter that limited King John's powers in England, six centuries before Napoleon's age.
Linked to Napoleon Bonaparte.Mayflower: Trap: the ship that carried the Pilgrims to Massachusetts in 1620, long before Napoleon was born.
Linked to Napoleon Bonaparte.Joan of Arc: Trap: a French heroine of the 1400s who rallied armies against England. Napoleon admired her, but she was 350 years earlier.
Linked to Napoleon Bonaparte.Henry VIII: Trap: the Tudor king of the 1500s, who married six times. He lived over two centuries before Napoleon.
Linked to Napoleon Bonaparte.Eiffel Tower: Trap: Paris's iron tower, built for the 1889 World's Fair. Napoleon died in 1821, so he never saw it.
Linked to Napoleon Bonaparte.Bannockburn: Trap: Robert the Bruce's 1314 victory over the English, five hundred years before Napoleon's era. Napoleon never fought there.
Linked to Napoleon Bonaparte.Little Bighorn: Trap: the 1876 battle in Montana in which Custer's force was wiped out, long after Napoleon's death.
Linked to Napoleon Bonaparte.Statue of Liberty: Trap: France gave it to the US in 1886, sixty-five years after Napoleon died, so it can't be linked to him.
