Real famous horses (not fictional).Marengo: Napoleon's gray Arabian; his skeleton is displayed at the National Army Museum in London.
Real famous horses (not fictional).Copenhagen: The Duke of Wellington rode him for about 17 hours at Waterloo, then he kicked at the Duke.
Real famous horses (not fictional).Traveller: Robert E. Lee's gray American Saddlebred was buried near Lee Chapel in Virginia.
Real famous horses (not fictional).Incitatus: Caligula's horse, who was supposedly set to be made consul, probably as a joke aimed at the Senate.
Real famous horses (not fictional).Comanche: The only US Army survivor found on the Little Bighorn battlefield, he spent his later years as a regimental mascot.
Real famous horses (not fictional).Seabiscuit: A small, scruffy racehorse who beat War Admiral in a 1938 match race and became a Depression hero.
Real famous horses (not fictional).Secretariat: He won the 1973 Belmont Stakes by 31 lengths in 2:24, a record that still stands, and his heart was reportedly oversized.
Real famous horses (not fictional).Red Rum: He won the Grand National three times, in 1973, 1974 and 1977.
Real famous horses (not fictional).Phar Lap: An Australian champion of the early 1930s who died suddenly in 1932, and his heart is displayed in Canberra.
Real famous horses (not fictional).Sergeant Reckless: A Korean War packhorse who carried ammunition under fire in 1953 and was promoted to staff sergeant.
Real famous horses (not fictional).Pegasus: Not real: Pegasus is the winged horse of Greek myth that sprang from Medusa's blood.
Real famous horses (not fictional).Sleipnir: Odin's eight-legged horse in Norse myth, so very much a legend.
Real famous horses (not fictional).Black Beauty: Black Beauty is the narrator of Anna Sewell's 1877 novel, so he is fictional.
Real famous horses (not fictional).Shadowfax: Gandalf's horse from The Lord of the Rings, the lord of all horses and fictional.
Real famous horses (not fictional).Rocinante: Don Quixote's old nag from Cervantes' novel, so not a real horse.
Real famous horses (not fictional).Boxer: The loyal cart horse in Orwell's Animal Farm, who works himself to death.
Real famous horses (not fictional).Maximus: The palace horse of Disney's Tangled is fictional, with the cunning of a bloodhound.
Real famous horses (not fictional).Artax: The Neverending Story's horse who sinks in the Swamp of Sadness is fictional.
Real famous horses (not fictional).Bullseye: Woody's horse in Toy Story 2 is a toy, not a real horse.
Real famous horses (not fictional).Joey: Joey is the war horse of Michael Morpurgo's 1982 novel, so he is fictional.
Real famous horses (not fictional).Silver: The Lone Ranger's horse, fictional, and he was a white stallion.
Real famous horses (not fictional).Epona: Zelda's horse is named for a Celtic horse goddess and is not real.
Real famous horses (not fictional).Black Stallion: Walter Farley's 1941 novel gave us the Black Stallion, so he is fictional.

Food a medieval European peasant might e.Bread: Coarse dark loaves made from rye or barley supplied much of the daily calories, and stale slabs served as plates called trenchers.
Food a medieval European peasant might e.Pottage: A thick stew of grain and vegetables that simmered over the hearth, with new bits added day by day.
Food a medieval European peasant might e.Cabbage: A winter staple that stored well, grown in nearly every cottage garden.
Food a medieval European peasant might e.Turnips: A root vegetable that stored all winter and fed Europe before the potato.
Food a medieval European peasant might e.Onions: A cheap flavoring for the pot, along with garlic, and found in almost every cottage garden.
Food a medieval European peasant might e.Barley: Cheaper than wheat and hardy in the cold, it fed people in porridge, bread and ale.
Food a medieval European peasant might e.Ale: Brewed at home, often by women called alewives, it was weak, and everyone drank it daily.
Food a medieval European peasant might e.Cheese: Mostly from sheep or goat milk, these dairy foods were called 'white meats' and sustained peasants.
Food a medieval European peasant might e.Peas: Dried peas kept all winter and supplied precious protein, hence the rhyme 'pease porridge hot'.
Food a medieval European peasant might e.Fava beans: Before the American beans arrived, this was Europe's main bean, also known as broad beans.
Food a medieval European peasant might e.Eggs: Hens were kept by cottages, but Lent rules restricted eggs for weeks.
Food a medieval European peasant might e.Leeks: Leeks made a staple soup, and they are now Wales's national emblem.
Food a medieval European peasant might e.Potatoes: Potatoes come from the Andes and reached Europe only after the 1500s.
Food a medieval European peasant might e.Tomatoes: Native to the Americas, tomatoes reached Europe only after Columbus.
Food a medieval European peasant might e.Maize: Maize is native to Mexico and came to Europe after 1492.
Food a medieval European peasant might e.Chocolate: Aztecs and Maya drank it, and it reached Europe in the 1500s.
Food a medieval European peasant might e.Coffee: Coffee came from Ethiopia and Arabia, and reached Europe in the 1600s.
Food a medieval European peasant might e.Pineapple: A South American fruit that was a luxury in 1600s Europe.
Food a medieval European peasant might e.Chili peppers: Native to the Americas, chili peppers reached Europe after Columbus; the medieval spice was black pepper.
Food a medieval European peasant might e.Peanuts: Peanuts come from South America, so a medieval peasant never tasted them.
Food a medieval European peasant might e.Avocado: Avocados come from Mesoamerica, so European peasants had never seen one.
Food a medieval European peasant might e.Tea: Tea comes from China and reached Europe in the 1600s.
Food a medieval European peasant might e.Vanilla: A Mexican orchid, first used by Mesoamerican peoples and only later in Europe.
Food a medieval European peasant might e.Green beans: Common green beans are American, and medieval Europe had fava beans.

Valid Roman numerals.XIV: The 14 uses subtractive notation (X then IV), and it's also the number of Louis XIV, the Sun King of France. Clocks often write 4 as IIII.
Valid Roman numerals.MCM: 1900, written M for 1000 and CM for 900, a form that famously appears in copyright dates of old films.
Valid Roman numerals.IX: IX is 9, and one of just six permitted subtractive pairs: IV, IX, XL, XC, CD and CM. Roman numerals have no zero and no place value.
Valid Roman numerals.XL: 40 is X before L, and XL is also the clothing size 'extra large'. Roman numerals have no zero and no place value.
Valid Roman numerals.CD: 400 is C before D, and CD is also short for compact disc. Roman numerals have no zero and no place value.
Valid Roman numerals.DCCC: 800 is D plus three Cs, and the standard form never stacks more than three alike symbols. Roman numerals have no zero and no place value.
Valid Roman numerals.MMXXIV: 2024 is simply MM, XX and IV added together, as the symbols sum from the biggest to the smallest.
Valid Roman numerals.LXX: 70 is L plus XX, and the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament, is abbreviated LXX for its legendary 70 translators.
Valid Roman numerals.CCC: 300 is just three Cs, which is as many repeats as the rules allow of a single symbol. Roman numerals have no zero and no place value.
Valid Roman numerals.XC: 90 is written as X before C, and XC is one of the few permitted subtractive pairs. Roman numerals have no zero and no place value.
Valid Roman numerals.VII: 7 is V plus two Is, and Henry VII, born in 1457, founded the Tudor dynasty. Roman numerals have no zero and no place value.
Valid Roman numerals.MDCLXVI: 1666, the year of the Great Fire of London, uses every Roman symbol exactly once in descending order.
Valid Roman numerals.VX: V is never subtracted, so 5 is just V and 10 is simply X. Roman numerals have no zero and no place value.
Valid Roman numerals.IL: I may precede only V or X, so 49 is written XLIX rather than IL. Roman numerals have no zero and no place value.
Valid Roman numerals.IC: I may precede only V or X, so 99 is written XCIX, not IC. Roman numerals have no zero and no place value.
Valid Roman numerals.XM: X may precede only L or C, so 990 is written CMXC, not XM. Roman numerals have no zero and no place value.
Valid Roman numerals.VV: V is never repeated, because two Vs is simply X. Roman numerals have no zero and no place value.
Valid Roman numerals.LL: L is never repeated, because two Ls is simply C. Roman numerals have no zero and no place value.
Valid Roman numerals.DD: D is never repeated, because two Ds is simply M. Roman numerals have no zero and no place value.
Valid Roman numerals.IIX: 8 is written VIII, since subtraction uses just a single smaller numeral, never two. Roman numerals have no zero and no place value.
Valid Roman numerals.VL: V is never used for subtraction, so 45 is written XLV. Roman numerals have no zero and no place value.
Valid Roman numerals.XD: 490 is written CDXC, because X may not precede D. Roman numerals have no zero and no place value.
Valid Roman numerals.LC: L is never subtracted, so 50 is simply L. Roman numerals have no zero and no place value.
Valid Roman numerals.IM: 999 is written CMXCIX, because I may precede only V or X. Roman numerals have no zero and no place value.

Things that usually run on batteries.TV remote: Infrared remotes flash invisible light in coded pulses, and a phone camera can usually show the blink that your eyes miss.
Things that usually run on batteries.Smoke detector: Most ionization models contain a speck of americium-241, and testing monthly matters because dead batteries are a top reason alarms fail.
Things that usually run on batteries.Flashlight: Britons say torch and Americans say flashlight, a name from early bulbs and batteries that could only flash briefly.
Things that usually run on batteries.Hearing aid: Most use zinc-air cells, which switch on only when you peel off the sticker and let oxygen in, so the clock starts then.
Things that usually run on batteries.Car key fob: A small coin cell such as the CR2032 usually powers it, and a weak battery is the usual reason it suddenly stops unlocking.
Things that usually run on batteries.Wireless mouse: Many run on a single AA, and low-energy Bluetooth lets some wireless mice go for months on one battery.
Things that usually run on batteries.Digital thermometer: Its circuit sips so little power that a tiny button cell often lasts for years of fever checks.
Things that usually run on batteries.Game controller: Wireless pads use AA cells or rechargeable packs, trading cords for the occasional battery swap in the middle of a game.
Things that usually run on batteries.Bathroom scale: Most hide a coin cell or AAA batteries, while strain gauges inside flex slightly to measure your weight.
Things that usually run on batteries.Wall clock: Quartz clocks keep time with a tiny crystal that vibrates 32,768 times a second, powered by a single AA for a year or more.
Things that usually run on batteries.Calculator: Many pocket models add a small solar cell, with a button battery as backup for dim rooms.
Things that usually run on batteries.Toaster: Heating elements demand roughly 800 to 1,500 watts, far more than any ordinary battery can deliver for more than a moment.
Things that usually run on batteries.Kettle: Boiling one liter takes about 300 kilojoules, more than dozens of AA batteries hold, which is why kettles plug into the wall.
Things that usually run on batteries.Fridge: A compressor needs steady mains power, though solar fridges in remote clinics do run from large battery banks.
Things that usually run on batteries.Microwave: A magnetron draws around 1,000 watts, so a microwave can't live on batteries without a bulky pack.
Things that usually run on batteries.Washing machine: Its motor, pump and heater need household current; no ordinary battery pack could run a full wash.
Things that usually run on batteries.Dishwasher: It heats water and pumps it at high power, and a dishwasher's cycle needs household current to finish.
Things that usually run on batteries.Oven: Even gas ovens need mains power for electronic ignition and controls, so a blackout can leave them stubbornly cold.
Things that usually run on batteries.Ceiling fan: Ceiling fans should spin counter-clockwise in summer to push air down, but they plug into the wall, not batteries.
Things that usually run on batteries.Hair dryer: Dryers draw 1,000 watts or more through a heating coil, far more than batteries could supply for long.
Things that usually run on batteries.Clothes iron: Cordless irons are only partly cordless: a heated base station supplies the energy, not a battery in the iron.
Things that usually run on batteries.Space heater: Space heaters typically use 1,500 watts, about the most a standard US outlet circuit comfortably supplies.
Things that usually run on batteries.Tumble dryer: Heat-pump dryers recycle warm air to save energy, yet they still need mains power.
Things that usually run on batteries.Chest freezer: A chest freezer's lid traps cold air because cold sinks, so less escapes when you open it, but it still plugs in.

Baking equipment.Rolling pin: French rolling pins are tapered batons with no handles, which lets bakers feel the dough thickness through their palms.
Baking equipment.Cookie cutter: Gingerbread shapes trace back to European tradition, and Queen Elizabeth I reputedly had gingerbread likenesses made of her guests.
Baking equipment.Piping bag: Swap the nozzle and the same icing makes stars, rosettes or petals, which is why decorators keep dozens of tips.
Baking equipment.Muffin tin: Dark metal tins brown muffins faster than light ones, so a recipe's time often depends on the tin you own.
Baking equipment.Cake tin: British recipes say 'tin' where Americans say 'pan', so the same cake can start with different vocabulary.
Baking equipment.Pastry brush: Brushing egg wash on pastry before baking gives the glossy golden crust you see in bakery windows.
Baking equipment.Flour sifter: Sifting aerates flour and breaks up lumps, though most modern flour needs it far less than recipes of old assume.
Baking equipment.Cooling rack: A raised rack lets air circulate under baked goods, so the bottoms do not steam and turn soggy.
Baking equipment.Loaf pan: A Pullman pan has a sliding lid, which bakes bread into the perfect square slices used for sandwiches.
Baking equipment.Pie dish: A glass pie dish lets you check the bottom crust is browned, the usual trouble spot for soggy pie.
Baking equipment.Bench scraper: This flat blade cuts dough, scrapes the counter clean and scoops chopped ingredients, doing several jobs at once.
Baking equipment.Wok: Its curved shape concentrates heat at the bottom, and the smoky flavor of great stir-fry is called wok hei, 'breath of the wok'.
Baking equipment.Garlic press: Crushing garlic releases more of its sharp compound, allicin, so pressed cloves taste harsher than sliced ones.
Baking equipment.Corkscrew: The waiter's friend corkscrew folds a knife for cutting foil, a design patented in the 1880s that is still the standard.
Baking equipment.Ladle: Ladles belong to the soup pot rather than the oven, though some bakers use them to pour pancake batter evenly.
Baking equipment.Potato masher: Mashers are for the stove, and they crush potatoes roughly, while a ricer gives a much fluffier mash.
Baking equipment.Can opener: Tin cans were invented around 1810, but the can opener came decades later, and soldiers once hacked cans open with bayonets.
Baking equipment.Salad spinner: It uses centrifugal force to fling water off greens, and dry leaves hold dressing far better than wet ones.
Baking equipment.Tongs: Tongs were among the earliest tools for handling fire, and today they are a grill favorite rather than a baking one.
Baking equipment.Chopsticks: Chopsticks have been used in China for over 3,000 years, and they are a table utensil, not a bakery one.
Baking equipment.Pepper grinder: Pepper's bite comes from piperine, and grinding fresh releases aromas that pre-ground pepper loses on the shelf.
Baking equipment.Ice cube tray: It is made to freeze water, but silicone trays also freeze stock, herbs or small chocolates in neat portions.
Baking equipment.Steamer basket: Steaming cooks gently, and stacked bamboo baskets are how dim sum is served throughout southern China.
Baking equipment.Meat cleaver: The Chinese cleaver, caidao, is actually a thin all-purpose knife for vegetables, not a bone-chopping meat tool.

Things usually made of ceramic.Toilet: Most toilets are vitreous china, fired above 1,000 degrees Celsius, which makes the surface glassy and nonporous.
Things usually made of ceramic.Teacup: Bone china contains bone ash, which makes it strong yet so thin that you can see light through it.
Things usually made of ceramic.Dinner plate: Before ceramic plates became common, many people ate from pewter, wood or even stale bread trenchers.
Things usually made of ceramic.Terracotta pot: Terracotta means 'baked earth' in Italian, and an unglazed pot breathes, so soil dries faster than in plastic.
Things usually made of ceramic.Bathroom sink: A porcelain sink is glazed so the surface is smooth and hard enough to resist stains, scratching and bacteria.
Things usually made of ceramic.Floor tile: Glazed ceramic tiles were made in Mesopotamia thousands of years ago, and fired clay is still a reliable flooring.
Things usually made of ceramic.Mug: Ceramic mugs hold heat well, and the glaze on the inside keeps the clay from absorbing coffee.
Things usually made of ceramic.Teapot: Porcelain was nicknamed white gold in Europe, where Meissen built the first hard-paste porcelain factory in 1710.
Things usually made of ceramic.Ramekin: The word is French, and these small glazed dishes are made for souffles and crème brulée since ceramic heats evenly.
Things usually made of ceramic.Saucer: People in earlier centuries sometimes poured hot tea into the saucer to cool it, and drank from that.
Things usually made of ceramic.Gravy boat: These are usually porcelain or earthenware, designed with a lip so sauce pours neatly onto food.
Things usually made of ceramic.Window: A window is glass, which is melted sand, not baked clay, and that is the key difference from ceramic.
Things usually made of ceramic.Wine glass: Glass is melted sand cooled quickly, whereas ceramic is fired clay, which explains why glass is clear and ceramic is opaque.
Things usually made of ceramic.Tin can: Tin cans are steel coated with tin, so they are metal through and through.
Things usually made of ceramic.Spatula: Spatulas are usually silicone, nylon, wood or metal, since ceramic would chip or crack under stirring.
Things usually made of ceramic.Paper plate: Paper plates are pressed paperboard, often with a coating, and are made to be thrown away.
Things usually made of ceramic.Plastic cup: Plastic cups are molded polymer, which is lighter and far less breakable than ceramic.
Things usually made of ceramic.Frying pan: Ceramic-coated pans exist, but they are metal pans with a thin silica-based coating, not solid ceramic.
Things usually made of ceramic.Drinking straw: The first drinking straws were rye grass stems, and the paper straw was patented in 1888 by Marvin Stone.
Things usually made of ceramic.Light bulb: A bulb is glass around a filament, though the socket or base can include ceramic as an insulator.
Things usually made of ceramic.Mirror: A mirror is glass with a reflective metal backing, and it has nothing to do with clay.
Things usually made of ceramic.Cutting board: Cutting boards are wood, plastic or bamboo, because a ceramic board would dull knives badly.
Things usually made of ceramic.Thermos: The vacuum flask was invented by Scottish scientist James Dewar in 1892, with a double wall of glass or steel.
Things usually made of ceramic.Ice cube tray: Ice cube trays are plastic, silicone or metal, which can flex or conduct cold, and ceramic cannot.

Things that have teeth.Comb: A comb's teeth are the thin prongs, and the oldest known combs are around 5,000 years old, made of bone and wood.
Things that have teeth.Saw: A saw's teeth are set alternately left and right so the cut is wider than the blade, which stops it from jamming.
Things that have teeth.Zipper: The zipper's interlocking teeth were refined in the 1910s by Gideon Sundback, and the word zipper came from B.F. Goodrich boots.
Things that have teeth.Shark: Sharks replace their teeth constantly, and some species can make tens of thousands over a lifetime.
Things that have teeth.Gear: A gear's teeth mesh with another gear's, and the ratio of teeth sets the speed of a machine, from clocks to bicycles.
Things that have teeth.Crocodile: A crocodile has around 60 to 70 teeth and can replace each one up to dozens of times over its life.
Things that have teeth.Beaver: A beaver's front teeth never stop growing, and their orange color comes from iron in the enamel that makes them tough.
Things that have teeth.Horse: You can estimate a horse's age by its teeth, which is why the phrase don't look a gift horse in the mouth exists.
Things that have teeth.Chainsaw: Chainsaw teeth are cutters on a chain that wraps around a bar and move at high speed, taking out chips of wood.
Things that have teeth.Dog: Adult dogs have 42 teeth compared with a person's 32, and puppies are born with none and grow 28 baby teeth.
Things that have teeth.Walrus: A walrus's tusks are enlarged canine teeth, up to a meter long, and it uses them to haul itself onto ice.
Things that have teeth.Human: People grow 20 baby teeth and then 32 adult teeth, and tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the human body.
Things that have teeth.Chicken: Chickens have no teeth, so they swallow small stones into a muscular gizzard, which grinds their food for them.
Things that have teeth.Turtle: Turtles have no teeth; a sharp horny beak does the cutting, and some species are strong enough to snap through bone.
Things that have teeth.Spoon: A spoon has a smooth bowl and no teeth; the fork, its cousin, has tines, which are sometimes loosely called teeth.
Things that have teeth.Anteater: Anteaters have no teeth at all; a sticky tongue up to about 60 centimeters long flicks in and out to slurp up ants.
Things that have teeth.Duck: Ducks have no true teeth, but a duck bill has small comb-like ridges on its edges that filter food from the water.
Things that have teeth.Ladle: A ladle has a deep bowl for scooping soup, and no teeth, though the bowl's rim is smooth and made for pouring.
Things that have teeth.Owl: Owls have no teeth, so they swallow prey whole and later cough up pellets of fur and bones.
Things that have teeth.Blue whale: The blue whale has no teeth; instead it filters tiny krill through baleen plates, eating several tons a day.
Things that have teeth.Pencil: A pencil has no teeth, though a chewed one gets bite marks; its core is graphite mixed with clay, never lead.
Things that have teeth.Sponge: A sponge is soft and riddled with holes, but those are pores, not teeth; real sponges are simple animals that filter water.
Things that have teeth.Eagle: Eagles have no teeth; a hooked beak tears meat, and powerful talons do the grabbing and killing.
Things that have teeth.Parrot: A parrot has no teeth, but its curved beak and strong jaw muscles can crack the hardest nuts, such as Brazil nuts.

Musicians in a symphony orchestra.Conductor: The conductor shapes tempo and expression with a baton, and their gestures guide dozens of players without a single word.
Musicians in a symphony orchestra.Violinist: Violinists form the largest section, often over 30 players, and they usually carry the melody.
Musicians in a symphony orchestra.Cellist: Cellists play an instrument held between the knees, and its range is close to the human voice.
Musicians in a symphony orchestra.Oboist: Oboists tune the orchestra, because the oboe's pitch is steady and cuts through, and every player tunes to its A.
Musicians in a symphony orchestra.Timpanist: A timpanist plays the large kettledrums, which can be tuned to exact pitches, so the job needs a good ear.
Musicians in a symphony orchestra.Harpist: A harpist plays one of the oldest instruments, with 47 strings and seven pedals that change pitch.
Musicians in a symphony orchestra.Flautist: Flautists play a flute, which was once made of wood and is now usually metal, even though it's still counted a woodwind.
Musicians in a symphony orchestra.Bassoonist: Bassoonists play a double-reed instrument about 2.5 metres long if unwound, which gives rise to its nickname of the clown of the orchestra.
Musicians in a symphony orchestra.Concertmaster: The concertmaster is the lead first violinist, second only to the conductor, who leads the string section and tunes the orchestra.
Musicians in a symphony orchestra.Trombonist: Trombonists use a slide, not valves, to change pitch, so they must find each note by ear and arm position.
Musicians in a symphony orchestra.Clarinetist: Clarinetists play a single-reed instrument whose range spans over three octaves, and Mozart wrote a famous concerto for it.
Musicians in a symphony orchestra.Violist: Violists play an instrument slightly bigger and deeper than the violin, and orchestra humour loves to tease them, though the viola is vital to the harmony.
Musicians in a symphony orchestra.DJ: A DJ plays recorded music, and it's a modern art not found in a symphony orchestra.
Musicians in a symphony orchestra.Bagpiper: Bagpipers play pipes with a bag and drones. It's a folk instrument with an old military tradition, not an orchestral one.
Musicians in a symphony orchestra.Rapper: A rapper performs rhythmic spoken verse, a style born in New York in the 1970s, not an orchestral job.
Musicians in a symphony orchestra.Beatboxer: A beatboxer makes drum sounds with their mouth, and it's a one-person art form of hip-hop culture.
Musicians in a symphony orchestra.Kazoo player: A kazoo player uses a simple instrument that buzzes the voice, and it appeared in the mid-1800s, so it's far from classical.
Musicians in a symphony orchestra.Banjo player: Banjo players are best known in folk and bluegrass, and the banjo traces its roots to West African instruments.
Musicians in a symphony orchestra.Ukulele player: Ukulele players use a small Hawaiian instrument adapted from a Portuguese folk guitar brought by 1800s immigrants, not an orchestra staple.
Musicians in a symphony orchestra.Turntablist: A turntablist uses record players as instruments, and the art grew out of hip-hop DJs in the 1970s.
Musicians in a symphony orchestra.Harmonica player: A harmonica player uses a reed instrument held in the hands, and it's best known in blues and folk, not the orchestra.
Musicians in a symphony orchestra.Yodeler: Yodelers jump quickly between chest and head voice, a tradition from the Alps, and not part of a symphony orchestra.
Musicians in a symphony orchestra.Keytarist: A keytarist plays a keyboard slung like a guitar, which became popular in the 1980s, and not a classical instrument.
Musicians in a symphony orchestra.Didgeridoo player: A didgeridoo player uses an Aboriginal Australian wind instrument, thought to be among the oldest in the world.

Things you'd find in a post office.Stamps: The Penny Black of 1840 was the world's first adhesive postage stamp, showing a young Queen Victoria.
Things you'd find in a post office.Envelopes: Before cheap postage in the 1840s, letters were folded and sealed on their own, because an envelope counted as an extra sheet.
Things you'd find in a post office.Postal scale: Postage is priced by weight, so a few grams can push a letter into a higher rate band.
Things you'd find in a post office.Parcels: The word comes from Old French parcelle, meaning a small part, from when a parcel was a part of a larger whole.
Things you'd find in a post office.PO boxes: A rented locked box gives a stable mailing address, handy for travellers and small businesses.
Things you'd find in a post office.Mail slot: Novelist Anthony Trollope, a Post Office official, is credited with pushing roadside pillar boxes into use in Britain.
Things you'd find in a post office.Customs forms: They tell border officials what's inside an international parcel and what it's worth, so duties and bans can apply.
Things you'd find in a post office.Bubble wrap: Invented in 1957 as textured wallpaper, it became packaging when it was used to protect shipped IBM computers.
Things you'd find in a post office.Address labels: ZIP codes launched in the US in 1963 to speed sorting, and machines now read addresses automatically.
Things you'd find in a post office.Postcards: The first postcards appeared in Austria-Hungary in 1869 as plain cards with the postage already printed.
Things you'd find in a post office.Mailbags: Pony Express riders in 1860 carried mail in a leather saddle cover called a mochila, built to be swapped quickly.
Things you'd find in a post office.Stethoscope: Clinics use it, not post offices; the name combines Greek words for chest and examine.
Things you'd find in a post office.Fire pole: Firefighters slide down it from sleeping quarters to the engines; one is said to have first appeared in Chicago in 1878.
Things you'd find in a post office.Jury box: Courtrooms hold them; the English jury goes back centuries, and twelve jurors became standard in medieval England.
Things you'd find in a post office.Pulpit: It belongs in a church; the phrase 'bully pulpit' was coined by Theodore Roosevelt.
Things you'd find in a post office.Hay bale: Farmers stack them; a large round bale can weigh around half a tonne or more.
Things you'd find in a post office.Operating table: Surgery rooms use adjustable ones that tilt a patient to give surgeons the right angle.
Things you'd find in a post office.Car lift: Garages raise cars on them; a typical two-post lift can hoist a whole sedan about two metres.
Things you'd find in a post office.Pizza oven: A wood-fired oven can reach about 400 degrees Celsius, cooking a Neapolitan pizza in a minute or two.
Things you'd find in a post office.Hot tub: Hot tubs are usually kept at around 38 to 40 degrees Celsius, a spa feature, not a postal one.
Things you'd find in a post office.Ball pit: Found in children's play areas, where thousands of plastic balls hide lost socks and the occasional phone.
Things you'd find in a post office.Jail cell: Prisons have them, and a prison's own mail is often inspected before delivery.
Things you'd find in a post office.Treadmill: Victorian prisons used the original from 1818, invented by William Cubitt, to grind grain as punishment.
Things you'd find in a post office.Slot machine: The first, the Liberty Bell, was built by Charles Fey in San Francisco around 1895.

Things in a vet's clinic.Exam table: Many have non-slip steel surfaces, and some lift hydraulically so a vet can examine a big dog without bending.
Things in a vet's clinic.Cone collar: Also called an Elizabethan collar, because it resembles the ruffled collars of Elizabethan fashion.
Things in a vet's clinic.Pet scale: Medication is dosed by body weight, so vets weigh pets accurately, especially small cats.
Things in a vet's clinic.Kennels: Kennel cough is a contagious bark-producing illness that spreads easily where dogs are housed together.
Things in a vet's clinic.Muzzle: A vet may use one on a frightened pet, because pain makes even gentle animals bite.
Things in a vet's clinic.Microchip scanner: The chip is about the size of a rice grain and holds an ID number, not a GPS location.
Things in a vet's clinic.Pet carrier: Leaving a carrier out at home lets cats see it as a normal resting place, making vet visits less stressful.
Things in a vet's clinic.Stethoscope: A cat's normal heart rate is far faster than ours, often 140 to 220 beats per minute.
Things in a vet's clinic.Flea treatment: Fleas can jump dozens of times their own length, and a female lays dozens of eggs a day, so treatment must be steady.
Things in a vet's clinic.Syringe: Doctors Alexander Wood and Charles Pravaz refined the hypodermic syringe in the 1850s.
Things in a vet's clinic.Dog treats: Vets keep treats handy, because dogs quickly learn to link a place with a reward.
Things in a vet's clinic.Barber pole: Its stripes recall when barber-surgeons performed bloodletting, and are nothing to do with pets.
Things in a vet's clinic.Pizza oven: The art of the Neapolitan pizza maker was added to UNESCO's heritage list in 2017.
Things in a vet's clinic.Slot machine: A casino gambling machine; the nickname 'one-armed bandit' refers to its single lever.
Things in a vet's clinic.Fire pole: Crews slide down it to save seconds, but a vet clinic has no need for one.
Things in a vet's clinic.Jukebox: Coin-operated music players peaked in the 1940s and 1950s; vets may play calm music, not a jukebox.
Things in a vet's clinic.Car lift: Garages raise cars to work underneath; a vet table lifts the pet, not the car.
Things in a vet's clinic.Pottery wheel: A potter's spinning platform, used for more than 5,000 years.
Things in a vet's clinic.Altar: A place of worship, though pets are blessed at church altars on the feast of St Francis, 4 October.
Things in a vet's clinic.Loom: A weaver's frame; wool comes from sheep that vets do treat, but the loom isn't clinic equipment.
Things in a vet's clinic.Ballot box: Australia introduced the secret ballot in the 1850s, which is why it's also called the Australian ballot.
Things in a vet's clinic.Trampoline: Invented by gymnast George Nissen in the 1930s; vets don't need one, even for energetic dogs.
Things in a vet's clinic.Espresso machine: The first was patented in Italy by Angelo Moriondo in 1884.
Things in a vet's clinic.Easel: An artist's frame, holding paintings rather than patients, however many pet portraits hang in the waiting room.

Written by Jane Austen.Emma: Austen's 1815 novel about a meddling matchmaker; she said she was creating a heroine 'whom no one but myself will much like'.
Written by Jane Austen.Persuasion: Published after her death in 1817, it follows Anne Elliot's second chance at love with a naval captain, and is her last complete novel.
Written by Jane Austen.Pride and Prejudice: Her best-known novel, first called First Impressions; it opens with the line about a single man in possession of a good fortune.
Written by Jane Austen.Northanger Abbey: A parody of Gothic novels, it was published after her death, along with Persuasion, though written much earlier.
Written by Jane Austen.Mansfield Park: Fanny Price, a poor relation raised by wealthy relatives, is the shy heroine of this 1814 novel; a famously quiet one.
Written by Jane Austen.Lady Susan: A short epistolary novel about a scheming widow, written around 1794 and not published until 1871.
Written by Jane Austen.Sanditon: Austen left this unfinished at her death in 1817; it's set in a seaside resort being developed as a spa town.
Written by Jane Austen.The Watsons: Austen abandoned this unfinished novel around 1805, about a family fallen into hardship.
Written by Jane Austen.Sense & Sensibility: Her 1811 debut, published anonymously 'By a Lady', follows two sisters who balance heart and head; she earned little from it at first.
Written by Jane Austen.Jane Eyre: Charlotte Brontë's 1847 novel; not by Austen, whose books are gentle comedies of manners.
Written by Jane Austen.Wuthering Heights: Emily Brontë's one novel is a dark tale of obsession, far from Austen's drawing rooms.
Written by Jane Austen.Middlemarch: George Eliot's Middlemarch is a Victorian epic, written long after Austen died.
Written by Jane Austen.Little Women: Louisa May Alcott's American Civil War-era classic about four sisters; Austen never wrote about America.
Written by Jane Austen.Vanity Fair: Thackeray's satire, from 1847-48, follows Becky Sharp; Austen is not its author.
Written by Jane Austen.Rebecca: Daphne du Maurier's 1938 gothic starts with 'Last night I dreamt I went to Manderley again.'
Written by Jane Austen.Cranford: Elizabeth Gaskell wrote this 1853 gentle tale of a small town ruled by women; it is not by Austen.
Written by Jane Austen.North and South: Gaskell's 1855 novel about a southern girl in a northern mill town is not by Austen.
Written by Jane Austen.Villette: Charlotte Brontë's last novel, from 1853, is not by Austen.
Written by Jane Austen.Clarissa: Samuel Richardson's 1748 epic, one of the longest English novels, was published decades before Austen.
Written by Jane Austen.Evelina: Fanny Burney's 1778 debut, which Austen admired, is not by her, though it influenced her.
Written by Jane Austen.Silas Marner: George Eliot's 1861 tale of a weaver is Victorian, and not by Austen.
Written by Jane Austen.Agnes Grey: Sir Walter Scott's 1819 medieval romance of knights and Robin Hood was hugely popular in her era, but it isn't hers.
Written by Jane Austen.Ivanhoe: Anne Brontë's 1847 novel about a governess, drawn from her own experience, is not Austen's.
Written by Jane Austen.Frankenstein: Mary Shelley's 1818 novel was published the year after Austen's death, and is Gothic science fiction, not comedy of manners.

Spanish artists.Pablo Picasso: Born in Málaga, he co-founded Cubism and was baptized with a name of more than twenty words.
Spanish artists.Salvador Dalí: The Catalan Surrealist behind The Persistence of Memory, whose upturned moustache became as famous as his melting clocks.
Spanish artists.Francisco Goya: Court painter who went deaf after an illness and later made the haunting Black Paintings on his own walls.
Spanish artists.Diego Velázquez: His 1656 Las Meninas fascinated Picasso, who painted 58 variations of it in 1957; Velázquez even paints himself in.
Spanish artists.Joan Miró: Catalan painter whose playful, dreamlike symbols and bright primary colors fill his canvases.
Spanish artists.Murillo: A Seville Baroque painter of tender Immaculate Conceptions and ragged street children; one of Spain's most beloved.
Spanish artists.Zurbarán: Seville painter of monks and still lifes with stark light; called the Spanish Caravaggio.
Spanish artists.Joaquín Sorolla: Valencian 'painter of light', famous for sunlit beach scenes of children and bathers.
Spanish artists.Juan Gris: Madrid-born Cubist who lived in Paris and took a name meaning 'grey'; he was born José Victoriano González-Pérez.
Spanish artists.Frida Kahlo: A Mexican, famed for self-portraits and painting her pain; she spoke Spanish but was not from Spain.
Spanish artists.Diego Rivera: A Mexican muralist, and Frida Kahlo's husband, so he is not Spanish, though he spoke the same language.
Spanish artists.Fernando Botero: A Colombian artist known for plump, inflated figures, so he is Latin American, not Spanish.
Spanish artists.Caravaggio: An Italian Baroque master of dramatic light, who spent part of his life on the run and was not Spanish.
Spanish artists.Titian: A Venetian, so Italian, though he painted for Spain's King Philip II for decades, which is the trap here.
Spanish artists.Claude Monet: A French Impressionist who painted water lilies at Giverny, so he is not Spanish.
Spanish artists.Rubens: A Flemish painter who visited Madrid in 1628 and befriended Velázquez, but he was not Spanish.
Spanish artists.Modigliani: An Italian painter in Paris, known for elongated faces and necks, so not Spanish.
Spanish artists.René Magritte: A Belgian Surrealist known for bowler hats and apples, and for 'This is not a pipe'.
Spanish artists.Marc Chagall: A Belarus-born painter, later French, of floating dreamlike lovers; he is not Spanish.
Spanish artists.Henri Matisse: A French Fauvist who used wild colors and cut-out paper in his late years; not Spanish.
Spanish artists.Paul Cézanne: French post-Impressionist who said he wanted to treat nature through cylinders, spheres and cones.
Spanish artists.Edgar Degas: A French painter famed for ballet dancers, who lost much of his sight late in life.
Spanish artists.Gustav Klimt: An Austrian Symbolist painter of gold-covered figures, born in Vienna.
Spanish artists.Edvard Munch: A Norwegian painter of The Scream, born in Norway; not Spanish.

Fictional schools from books.Hogwarts: Hogwarts is the Scottish school of witchcraft and wizardry in Harry Potter, and its name isn't tied to a real place.
Fictional schools from books.Beauxbatons: Beauxbatons is the French wizarding school in Goblet of Fire, whose students arrive in a carriage pulled by giant winged horses.
Fictional schools from books.Durmstrang: Durmstrang is the northern wizarding school in Goblet of Fire, with a name that plays on the German Sturm und Drang.
Fictional schools from books.Malory Towers: Malory Towers is Enid Blyton's girls' boarding school series, starring Darrell Rivers, and it's set on a Cornish cliff.
Fictional schools from books.Wayside School: Wayside School is Louis Sachar's school built sideways by mistake, with thirty classrooms stacked in a tower.
Fictional schools from books.Crunchem Hall: Crunchem Hall is the primary school where Miss Trunchbull terrorizes children in Dahl's Matilda.
Fictional schools from books.Dotheboys Hall: Dotheboys Hall is Dickens's cruel Yorkshire school in Nicholas Nickleby, which helped expose such institutions.
Fictional schools from books.Lowood: Lowood is the harsh charity school in Jane Eyre, based on the one Brontë's sisters attended.
Fictional schools from books.Pencey Prep: Pencey Prep is the school Holden Caulfield is expelled from in The Catcher in the Rye, after failing four of five classes.
Fictional schools from books.Unseen University: Unseen University is the wizard school in Pratchett's Discworld, where the Librarian is an orangutan.
Fictional schools from books.Eton: Eton College is a real school founded in 1440 by Henry VI, and many British prime ministers studied there.
Fictional schools from books.Harvard: Harvard is a real university, founded in 1636 and named for John Harvard, who left it his books.
Fictional schools from books.Oxford: Oxford is a real university, teaching there since about 1096, making it the oldest in the English-speaking world.
Fictional schools from books.Yale: Yale is a real university in New Haven, named after a donor, Elihu Yale, who gave books and goods.
Fictional schools from books.Juilliard: Juilliard is a real performing-arts school in New York, founded in 1905, and not fictional.
Fictional schools from books.Sorbonne: The Sorbonne is a real Paris institution, named for Robert de Sorbon, who founded a college there in the 1250s.
Fictional schools from books.West Point: West Point is the real US Military Academy on the Hudson River, founded in 1802.
Fictional schools from books.Cambridge: Cambridge is a real university, founded around 1209 by scholars who left Oxford after a dispute.
Fictional schools from books.MIT: MIT is the real Massachusetts Institute of Technology, in Cambridge, Massachusetts, not a fictional school.
Fictional schools from books.Princeton: Princeton is a real New Jersey university, founded in 1746 as the College of New Jersey, so it's not fictional.
Fictional schools from books.Rugby School: Rugby School is real, and it's the setting of Tom Brown's School Days; it may have given rise to rugby.
Fictional schools from books.Stanford: Stanford is a real California university, founded in 1885 by Leland Stanford in memory of his son.
Fictional schools from books.Gordonstoun: Gordonstoun is a real Scottish boarding school that Prince Philip and Prince Charles attended.
Fictional schools from books.Brown: Brown is a real Rhode Island Ivy League university, founded in 1764, and it's not a fictional school.

Written by C. S. Lewis.Mere Christianity: It grew from BBC radio talks Lewis gave during World War II, when his voice was among the most listened-to in Britain.
Written by C. S. Lewis.The Four Loves: Lewis splits love into four Greek-named kinds: affection, friendship, romantic love (eros) and charity (agape).
Written by C. S. Lewis.Perelandra: The second book of his Space Trilogy sends a hero to Venus, where he faces a retelling of the Eden temptation.
Written by C. S. Lewis.The Great Divorce: A bus ride from hell to the edge of heaven; the title answers William Blake's The Marriage of Heaven and Hell.
Written by C. S. Lewis.Prince Caspian: The second Narnia book to be published (1951) has the Pevensies return to find that centuries have passed in Narnia.
Written by C. S. Lewis.The Silver Chair: This Narnia story introduces Puddleglum, a gloomy but loyal Marsh-wiggle, and the hunt for a lost prince.
Written by C. S. Lewis.Miracles: His 1947 argument that miracles are possible was revised after philosopher Elizabeth Anscombe challenged a chapter.
Written by C. S. Lewis.The Last Battle: It won the 1956 Carnegie Medal, the only Narnia book to win it, and ends the series with Narnia's end.
Written by C. S. Lewis.The Abolition of Man: Based on three 1943 lectures, it defends objective moral values against relativism; Lewis's novel That Hideous Strength echoes it.
Written by C. S. Lewis.A Grief Observed: Lewis published this raw account of his wife's death under the pseudonym N. W. Clerk in 1961.
Written by C. S. Lewis.Till We Have Faces: Lewis's retelling of Cupid and Psyche is told by Psyche's jealous sister; he considered it his best novel.
Written by C. S. Lewis.Surprised by Joy: His 1955 memoir of conversion centers on joy as a sudden longing; he'd later marry Joy Davidman.
Written by C. S. Lewis.The Hobbit: This belongs to Tolkien, Lewis's close friend in the Inklings, the Oxford writing group.
Written by C. S. Lewis.The Silmarillion: Tolkien's history of the elves was published only in 1977, after he died, edited by his son Christopher.
Written by C. S. Lewis.The Two Towers: Tolkien wrote The Two Towers; Lewis had encouraged him to finish The Lord of the Rings.
Written by C. S. Lewis.Farmer Giles of Ham: A comic tale by Tolkien, about a reluctant dragon-slaying farmer, published in 1949.
Written by C. S. Lewis.A Wrinkle in Time: Madeleine L'Engle wrote this 1962 science fantasy; it was rejected by dozens of publishers before publication.
Written by C. S. Lewis.The Golden Compass: Philip Pullman wrote this, called Northern Lights in Britain; it won the 1995 Carnegie Medal.
Written by C. S. Lewis.Watership Down: Richard Adams's rabbit epic began as stories told to his daughters on a car journey.
Written by C. S. Lewis.A Wizard of Earthsea: Ursula K. Le Guin's 1968 novel introduced Ged, a young wizard whose power teaches him humility.
Written by C. S. Lewis.Stardust: Neil Gaiman's 1999 fairy tale of a wall and a star is not Lewis's, though Narnia likewise lies behind a doorway.
Written by C. S. Lewis.Peter Pan: J. M. Barrie's boy who never grew up, a play (1904) and a novel from 1911.
Written by C. S. Lewis.The Little Prince: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry's 1943 fable of a boy from an asteroid is among the best-selling books ever.
Written by C. S. Lewis.Coraline: Neil Gaiman's 2002 novel about a girl and her button-eyed other mother, nothing from Narnia.

Musicals by Rodgers and Hammerstein.Oklahoma!: Their first collaboration in 1943 is generally considered the first 'integrated' musical, with songs driving the story.
Musicals by Rodgers and Hammerstein.Carousel: Rodgers called it his favorite of his own musicals, and it includes 'You'll Never Walk Alone'.
Musicals by Rodgers and Hammerstein.South Pacific: Won the 1950 Pulitzer Prize for Drama, and tackled racism in 'You've Got to Be Carefully Taught'.
Musicals by Rodgers and Hammerstein.The King and I: Yul Brynner played the king over 4,000 times, and the story comes from Anna Leonowens's memoirs of Siam, now Thailand.
Musicals by Rodgers and Hammerstein.The Sound of Music: Their final show opened in 1959; Hammerstein died the following year, and the film made it a worldwide favorite.
Musicals by Rodgers and Hammerstein.Cinderella: Written for TV in 1957, it starred Julie Andrews live and drew an enormous audience.
Musicals by Rodgers and Hammerstein.Flower Drum Song: It starred an almost entirely Asian-American cast, which was rare on Broadway in 1958.
Musicals by Rodgers and Hammerstein.State Fair: Their only musical written for the screen, it won an Oscar for 'It Might as Well Be Spring'.
Musicals by Rodgers and Hammerstein.Allegro: Allegro (1947) followed a doctor from birth to middle age, and used a Greek-style chorus, an experiment that mostly baffled audiences.
Musicals by Rodgers and Hammerstein.Me and Juliet: A little-remembered 1953 backstage musical about a theater company, whose best-known song is 'No Other Love'.
Musicals by Rodgers and Hammerstein.Pipe Dream: Based on John Steinbeck's novel Sweet Thursday, this 1955 show is set on Cannery Row.
Musicals by Rodgers and Hammerstein.West Side Story: Leonard Bernstein composed it, with lyrics by a young Stephen Sondheim; it's a Romeo and Juliet update in 1950s New York.
Musicals by Rodgers and Hammerstein.My Fair Lady: Lerner and Loewe's 1956 adaptation of Shaw's Pygmalion starred Julie Andrews, and was a huge Broadway hit.
Musicals by Rodgers and Hammerstein.Guys and Dolls: Frank Loesser wrote it based on Damon Runyon's stories of New York gamblers and their sweethearts.
Musicals by Rodgers and Hammerstein.Hello Dolly!: Jerry Herman's 1964 hit starred Carol Channing, and Louis Armstrong's recording of the title song hit number one, displacing the Beatles.
Musicals by Rodgers and Hammerstein.Cats: Andrew Lloyd Webber based it on T. S. Eliot's poems, and it ran in London for 21 years.
Musicals by Rodgers and Hammerstein.Evita: Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice's musical about Argentina's Eva Perón began as a concept album in 1976.
Musicals by Rodgers and Hammerstein.Fiddler on the Roof: Bock and Harnick's musical, set in a Jewish village in Tsarist Russia, ran for over 3,000 performances on its first Broadway run.
Musicals by Rodgers and Hammerstein.Cabaret: Kander and Ebb's musical, set in Berlin in 1931 as the Nazis rise, was based on Christopher Isherwood's stories.
Musicals by Rodgers and Hammerstein.Chicago: Kander and Ebb's show comes from a 1926 play by journalist Maurine Dallas Watkins, based on real Chicago murder trials.
Musicals by Rodgers and Hammerstein.Oliver!: Lionel Bart's musical adapts Dickens's Oliver Twist, and 'Consider Yourself' is one of its hits.
Musicals by Rodgers and Hammerstein.Grease: Jim Jacobs and Warren Casey's rock-and-roll musical started in Chicago before Broadway, and later became a hit film.
Musicals by Rodgers and Hammerstein.Annie: Charles Strouse and Martin Charnin's musical comes from a comic strip, Little Orphan Annie, and its song 'Tomorrow' is a classic.
Musicals by Rodgers and Hammerstein.The Music Man: Meredith Willson's 1957 show, set in a small Iowa town, features 'Seventy-Six Trombones' and the con man Harold Hill.

Things with teeth that aren't animals.Comb: Combs are very old; archaeologists have found ones made from bone and wood from thousands of years ago.
Things with teeth that aren't animals.Hand saw: Saw teeth are bent slightly outward, called the set, so the cut is wider than the blade and doesn't bind.
Things with teeth that aren't animals.Zipper: Whitcomb Judson patented an early version in 1893, but it was Gideon Sundback who made the modern one around 1913.
Things with teeth that aren't animals.Gear: Gear teeth are shaped in a curve called an involute so they mesh smoothly, and the shape keeps the speed ratio constant.
Things with teeth that aren't animals.Rake: The tines on a garden rake are sometimes called teeth, and they rake leaves and soil to loosen and level them.
Things with teeth that aren't animals.Key: A key's teeth, or bitting, lift the pins inside a lock to exactly the right height, and only the right pattern turns it.
Things with teeth that aren't animals.Chainsaw: Chainsaw teeth alternate left and right, so each cuts its own slice of wood, and they dull fast if they hit dirt.
Things with teeth that aren't animals.Bike sprocket: The teeth on a bike sprocket grip the chain, and the ratio of teeth between front and rear sets how hard a gear is to push.
Things with teeth that aren't animals.Hacksaw: A hacksaw's fine teeth are made for metal, and the number of teeth per inch is chosen to suit the thickness of the metal.
Things with teeth that aren't animals.Spoon: A spoon has no teeth, though a "spork" and the fork it combines with have prongs, which are called tines instead.
Things with teeth that aren't animals.Hammer: A hammer has a face and a claw, and while the claw grips nails, it has no teeth.
Things with teeth that aren't animals.Ruler: Rulers have tick marks, not teeth, though some pocket ones have a small serrated edge.
Things with teeth that aren't animals.Shovel: It is the digging blade of the shovel, which is all edge with no teeth, though some saw-edged garden tools do exist.
Things with teeth that aren't animals.Scissors: Scissors have blades, not teeth, though some pinking shears have zigzag edges to prevent fabric from fraying.
Things with teeth that aren't animals.Rope: Ropes are twisted fibres, and no teeth are involved, though a tight twist keeps the strands from coming apart.
Things with teeth that aren't animals.Mop: A mop is strands on a handle, so there is nothing to bite with.
Things with teeth that aren't animals.Broom: Broom bristles do the sweeping, and bristles are not teeth, even though they look similar in a row.
Things with teeth that aren't animals.Plate: A plate is a smooth dish, and chipped ones can have rough jagged edges, but not teeth.
Things with teeth that aren't animals.Pencil: A pencil's lead is graphite, not lead, and it has a wood body and no teeth.
Things with teeth that aren't animals.Screwdriver: A screwdriver has a tip shaped for the screw head, and the screw has threads, not teeth.
Things with teeth that aren't animals.Whisk: A whisk uses loops of wire to add air to eggs or cream, and they're called wires, not teeth.
Things with teeth that aren't animals.Ladder: A ladder has rungs, not teeth, though some folding ones lock with ratchet-like notches.
Things with teeth that aren't animals.Hose: A hose is a flexible tube and the threaded end screws on, so no teeth.
Things with teeth that aren't animals.Paintbrush: It has bristles, not teeth, and good ones hold paint by capillary action between the hairs.

Things bigger than an elephant.Blue whale: The blue whale is the largest animal ever known, up to about 30 meters long and weighing as much as roughly 25 elephants.
Things bigger than an elephant.Brachiosaurus: This long-necked dinosaur stood as tall as a four-story building, with front legs longer than its back legs, like a giraffe.
Things bigger than an elephant.Sperm whale: The sperm whale has the biggest brain of any animal, around five times heavier than a human's, and it dives over a kilometer deep to hunt squid.
Things bigger than an elephant.Whale shark: The biggest fish alive can top 12 meters, yet it eats plankton, and each shark has a spot pattern as unique as a fingerprint.
Things bigger than an elephant.Humpback whale: Humpbacks weigh around 30 tons or more, and males sing complex songs that spread across whole ocean basins.
Things bigger than an elephant.Redwood tree: Coast redwoods top 110 meters, taller than any other tree, and the tallest known, Hyperion, is about 116 meters.
Things bigger than an elephant.Cruise ship: The largest cruise ships weigh over 200,000 tons, many times heavier than a whole herd of elephants.
Things bigger than an elephant.Mount Everest: Everest rises about 8,849 meters above sea level, and it grows a few millimeters each year as the Indian plate pushes north.
Things bigger than an elephant.The Moon: The Moon is about a quarter of Earth's diameter and drifts away from us by around 3.8 centimeters every year.
Things bigger than an elephant.Boeing 747: The jumbo jet first flew in 1969, stretches over 70 meters in length, and its empty weight is many times that of a big elephant herd.
Things bigger than an elephant.Blimp: A blimp is a floating gasbag with no rigid frame, and the biggest ones are far longer than a house, while light for their size.
Things bigger than an elephant.Statue of Liberty: Lady Liberty stands about 93 meters from ground to torch, and her copper skin is only about two pennies thick, and turned green with age.
Things bigger than an elephant.Rhino: A white rhino can weigh up to about 2.3 tons, but an African elephant can weigh up to 6 tons, so it comes up short.
Things bigger than an elephant.Hippo: A hippo may weigh around 1.5 to 3 tons, heavy, but still smaller than the elephant, and it can outrun a human on land.
Things bigger than an elephant.Polar bear: The largest land carnivore, an adult male polar bear can weigh over 500 kilograms, but that is well under an elephant's weight.
Things bigger than an elephant.Moose: The largest deer in the world can weigh up to 700 kilograms and stand taller than a horse, yet it is still dwarfed by elephants.
Things bigger than an elephant.Gorilla: Silverback gorillas weigh up to about 200 kilograms, and are strong, but remain far smaller than any elephant.
Things bigger than an elephant.Horse: Horses weigh around 500 kilograms, about a tenth of a large African bull elephant.
Things bigger than an elephant.Crocodile: Saltwater crocodiles are the biggest reptiles, reaching about 1,000 kilograms, which is still well below an elephant.
Things bigger than an elephant.Bison: The American bison is North America's largest land mammal at up to a ton, and yet it is smaller than an elephant.
Things bigger than an elephant.Grizzly bear: A big grizzly can weigh 400 kilograms or more and stand over two meters when upright, yet it is much smaller than an elephant.
Things bigger than an elephant.Car: A typical car weighs about 1.5 tons, and a big bull elephant can weigh about four times that.
Things bigger than an elephant.Walrus: Walrus males weigh up to about 1.5 tons, but the tusked giant is still much lighter than an elephant.
Things bigger than an elephant.Lion: An adult male lion weighs about 190 kilograms, a fraction of an elephant, even though it is called king of the beasts.

Things that are rectangular.Door: Door proportions are close to a 1 to 2.5 ratio, tall and narrow, a size standard in most houses since medieval times.
Things that are rectangular.Book: Paperbacks, hardcovers and e-readers all use rectangles, because pages cut from rectangular sheets waste no paper.
Things that are rectangular.Brick: A standard brick is about twice as long as it is wide, so it can be laid in staggered patterns.
Things that are rectangular.Dollar bill: The US dollar bill has stayed the same size since 1929, at roughly 6 by 2.6 inches.
Things that are rectangular.Envelope: Envelopes are folded from a rectangle or near-rectangle, and the diamond-shaped flap helps seal them.
Things that are rectangular.Credit card: Credit cards follow an international standard, ID-1, which sets size at about 85 by 54 millimeters.
Things that are rectangular.TV screen: Most TVs use a 16 by 9 shape, chosen as a compromise between older TV and widescreen movie formats.
Things that are rectangular.Domino: A domino is twice as long as it is wide, so two squares sit side by side.
Things that are rectangular.Mattress: Standard mattress sizes such as queen and king are rectangles of set dimensions, so sheets fit all brands.
Things that are rectangular.Smartphone: Smartphones are rectangles with rounded corners, a look the iPhone helped popularize.
Things that are rectangular.Shoebox: A shoebox is a rectangular box, and the term is also a common size for model railway layouts and diorama projects.
